title: INFO inside MULTI/EXEC re-locks shards the transaction already holds: self-deadlock that hangs the server
description: exec_transaction locks the shards of every queued key command and every WATCHed key (cmd.rs:1556-1580). It then calls each handler directly while holding those guards (cmd.rs:1610). INFO has flags 0, so it is queued inside MULTI, which Valkey also allows because info.json has no NO_MULTI flag. cmd_info then calls `sh.store.lock(i)` for every shard 0..NSHARDS (cmd.rs:1957-1961). std::sync::Mutex is not reentrant. Locking a shard the current thread already holds never returns: with the futex implementation it deadlocks, and if it panics instead, release builds use panic=abort and the process dies. The stuck worker keeps the transaction's shard guards forever. Every other thread that later needs one of those shards also blocks: commands on keys in that shard, the cron of the worker that owns the shard (cmd.rs:605, run within 100 ms), evict_one picking it at random, and INFO/KEYS/DBSIZE/FLUSHALL, which lock all shards.
failure_scenario: Any authenticated client sends `MULTI`, `SET foo bar`, `INFO`, `EXEC`. Another trigger is `WATCH foo`, `MULTI`, `INFO keyspace`, `EXEC`. EXEC locks shard_of(foo). cmd_info reaches that shard index and blocks forever on its own lock. Within about 100 ms the cron of the worker that owns that shard blocks too, and so do all clients touching that shard or running INFO/KEYS/DBSIZE/FLUSHALL. The server stops answering and must be killed. Valkey returns [OK, <info text>].
suggested_fix: Do not take shard locks in cmd_info. Keep per-shard key and volatile counts in atomics published like `mem`, or read them through the guards already held in cx.locks when running inside EXEC. More generally, no handler run by exec_transaction should call Store::lock.
verifier_reasoning: INFO is spec flags 0 (cmd.rs:218), so run_command queues it inside MULTI (cmd.rs:408-419). Valkey's info.json flags are LOADING/STALE/SENTINEL with no NO_MULTI, so Valkey runs it. exec_transaction adds shard_of(foo) for a queued SET foo, or for any WATCHed key, to ids and locks it (cmd.rs:1556-1580). It then calls cmd_info directly with those guards held in Locks::Many (cmd.rs:1590-1610). cmd_info ignores cx.locks and calls sh.store.lock(i) for every i in 0..NSHARDS (cmd.rs:1957-1961). Store::lock is self.shards[shard].lock().unwrap() on a std Mutex (store.rs:112-113), which is not reentrant. On Linux the futex mutex blocks forever on re-lock by the same thread. The worker never returns, so its own connections and its cron stop too. It keeps the guards, so the cron of the thread that owns the shard (cmd.rs:605), evict_one, key commands on that shard, and the Keys::All commands all block. With MULTI, SET foo bar, INFO, EXEC this hangs; Valkey returns [OK, info]. If no shard is locked (MULTI, INFO, EXEC alone), it does not hang, but the reported scenarios do lock a shard.

title: UNWATCH queued inside MULTI self-deadlocks EXEC on the watched key's shard
description: UNWATCH has flags 0, so it is queued inside MULTI. Valkey also allows this because unwatch.json has no NO_MULTI flag. EXEC adds the shard of every key in conn.watched to the lock set (cmd.rs:1557-1558) and locks it (cmd.rs:1580). If the watch flag is clean, it runs cmd_unwatch (cmd.rs:1639-1641), which calls unwatch_all. unwatch_all calls `store.lock(Store::shard_of(h))` for each watched key (cmd.rs:110-111). Those are exactly the shards the same thread already holds, so the non-reentrant std Mutex never returns. The worker hangs holding the guards, and other workers pile up behind it as in the INFO case.
failure_scenario: A client sends `WATCH k`, `MULTI`, `UNWATCH`, `EXEC` with no concurrent write to k. EXEC locks shard_of(k), the flag is false, and the queued UNWATCH runs unwatch_all, which blocks forever on shard_of(k). The connection never gets a reply. Every other client that touches that shard, the cron that owns it, eviction, and INFO/KEYS/DBSIZE/FLUSHALL all hang. Valkey replies [OK].
suggested_fix: Inside EXEC, make UNWATCH avoid Store::lock. For example, defer it (EXEC calls unwatch_all after dropping the locks anyway), or unregister the watches through the guards already held in cx.locks.
verifier_reasoning: UNWATCH is spec flags 0 (cmd.rs:207), so it is queued inside MULTI. Valkey allows this: unwatch.json has no NO_MULTI, and Valkey's execCommand calls unwatchAllKeys before running the queue (multi.c:361), so a queued UNWATCH is a no-op. In rvk, exec_transaction locks shard_of(k) for every key in conn.watched (cmd.rs:1557-1558, 1580). If watch_flag is false it runs the handlers (cmd.rs:1610), and exec_transaction special-cases only exec and multi (cmd.rs:1607). cmd_unwatch calls unwatch_all (cmd.rs:1639-1641), which calls store.lock(shard_of(h)) for each watched key (cmd.rs:110-111). Those are the guards this thread already holds, so the non-reentrant std Mutex blocks forever. conn.watched is only drained after the loop (cmd.rs:1619), so the list is still full at that point. WATCH k, MULTI, UNWATCH, EXEC therefore self-deadlocks, and other workers then pile up behind the held shard as in finding 0.

title: MULTI/EXEC bypasses maxmemory: no OOM rejection and no eviction for transactional writes
description: In run_command, commands issued while conn.multi is set are queued and return QUEUED (cmd.rs:408-419) before the DENYOOM/make_room check at cmd.rs:421 is reached. EXEC itself has no DENYOOM flag, so make_room is not called for it either. exec_transaction runs the queued handlers directly (cmd.rs:1610), without make_room. Writes inside a transaction therefore never evict and are never refused. Valkey runs the OOM check before queueing (rejectCommand flags the transaction, giving EXECABORT). It also runs performEvictions for EXEC using the combined DENYOOM flags of the queued commands (server.c:4731, 4864-4881).
failure_scenario: Under `--maxmemory 64mb --maxmemory-policy noeviction` with memory at the limit, a plain `SET k v` returns -OOM. But looping `MULTI`, `SET k:N <1MB value>`, `EXEC` returns [OK] every time, and memory grows without bound until the process is OOM-killed. Under allkeys-lru, a client that wraps every write in a transaction (e.g. a redis-py pipeline, which uses transaction=True by default) never triggers eviction, so used memory climbs past maxmemory without limit.
suggested_fix: For DENYOOM commands, call make_room (no locks held) before queueing. On failure, reply -OOM and set m.errored. In run_command, before exec_transaction takes any locks, call make_room if any queued command is DENYOOM, and reply -OOM if it fails, as Valkey does.
verifier_reasoning: In run_command, the MULTI queueing branch (cmd.rs:408-419) returns QUEUED before the DENYOOM/make_room check at cmd.rs:421. EXEC's spec has only NOMULTI (cmd.rs:204), so make_room is not called for EXEC either, and exec_transaction calls spec.run directly with no make_room (cmd.rs:1610). make_room is the only eviction or OOM path: cron does not evict (cmd.rs:593-621), and grep shows make_room is called only at cmd.rs:421. Valkey calls performEvictions for every command when maxmemory is set (server.c:4869). For EXEC it ORs the queued commands' DENYOOM into is_denyoom_command (server.c:4722-4731, multi.c:133). A queued SET at OOM is rejected through rejectCommand, which flags the transaction. So under noeviction, transactional SETs are never refused and memory grows past maxmemory. Under allkeys-lru or allkeys-random, a client that writes only inside transactions never triggers eviction.

title: Watched key that logically expires before EXEC does not abort the transaction (lost WATCH invalidation)
description: The only abort condition EXEC checks is conn.watch_flag (cmd.rs:1581). The flag is set only when a key is physically modified or removed under the shard lock. A watched key whose TTL passes between WATCH and EXEC stays in the slab until cron or a lazy lookup removes it. When EXEC runs first, the flag is still false and the transaction commits. The queued command's own lazy expiry then sets the flag too late. Valkey's execCommand calls isWatchedKeyExpired (multi.c:325, 576-590): any watched key that was live at WATCH time and is logically expired at EXEC makes the client dirty. cmd_watch (cmd.rs:1622-1635) does not record whether a key was expired at WATCH time either.
failure_scenario: Run `SET k 5 PX 100`, then `WATCH k` and `GET k` (returns 5). Wait 150 ms, before cron pops k. That is deterministic with --threads 1 and `DEBUG SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE 0`. It also happens whenever k's shard is past the 25 ms cron budget or the 100 ms tick has not come yet. Then send `MULTI`, `SET k 6`, `EXEC`. rvk returns [OK] and commits a value computed from a key that no longer exists. Valkey returns a nil array. Valkey's test 'EXEC fail on lazy expired WATCHed key' (tests/unit/multi.tcl:254) fails.
suggested_fix: Store an expired-at-WATCH flag with each watched key. In exec_transaction, after taking the locks, look up each watched key's slot. If a key was live at WATCH time and its expire is now <= now, abort as on a dirty flag.
verifier_reasoning: exec_transaction aborts only when conn.watch_flag is set (cmd.rs:1581). The flag is set only through notify_watchers, from set, replace_value, set_expire, remove_at and clear (store.rs:192, 229, 239, 254, 293). A watched key past its TTL that cron and lazy lookup have not yet removed leaves the flag false. cmd_watch does not look up the key or record its expiry state (cmd.rs:1622-1635). The queued SET k 6 sets the flag only after the check. With --threads 1 and DEBUG SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE 0 (cmd.rs:2024-2027, a per-thread flag checked in cron at cmd.rs:598), SET k 5 PX 100, WATCH k, wait 150 ms, MULTI, SET k 6, EXEC returns [OK]. Valkey's execCommand calls isWatchedKeyExpired (multi.c:325, 576-590), which finds k logically expired and was not expired at WATCH time, so it returns a nil array.

title: FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB invalidates WATCH on keys that do not exist
description: Shard::clear notifies every key in the shard's watched map, whether or not the key exists (store.rs:290-294). Valkey's touchAllWatchedKeysInDb only dirties watchers of keys present in the emptied DB (multi.c:649-650). A flush therefore aborts transactions that watched absent keys, even though nothing they watched changed.
failure_scenario: A client sends `DEL x`, then `WATCH x`. Another client (or the same one) sends `FLUSHALL`. The first client then sends `MULTI`, `PING`, `EXEC`. rvk returns a nil array; Valkey returns [PONG]. Valkey's tests 'FLUSHALL does not touch non affected keys' and 'FLUSHDB does not touch non affected keys' (tests/unit/multi.tcl:361, 379) fail.
suggested_fix: In clear(), notify a watched key only when self.find(hash(key), key) finds it, before clearing the slab and index.
verifier_reasoning: Shard::clear iterates every key in self.watched and calls notify_watchers on it, without checking whether the key exists in the slab (store.rs:290-294). cmd_flushall calls clear() on every shard (cmd.rs:1510-1512). Valkey's touchAllWatchedKeysInDb only dirties a client when exists_in_emptied, or the key exists in replaced_with (multi.c:649-650). So DEL x, WATCH x, FLUSHALL, MULTI, PING, EXEC gives a nil array in rvk and [PONG] in Valkey, which is what tests/unit/multi.tcl 'FLUSHALL does not touch non affected keys' expects.

title: Deleting a key that was already expired when WATCHed spuriously aborts EXEC
description: remove_at always calls notify_watchers_at (store.rs:254), including when the removal is lazy expiry (store.rs:173-174), cron expire_due (store.rs:324) or clear() of a key that was already stale when the client watched it. cmd_watch does not record stale-at-WATCH state. Valkey's touchWatchedKey skips watchers whose wk->expired is set when the stale key is deleted, because nothing changed logically (multi.c:609-615). The same applies in touchAllWatchedKeysInDb (multi.c:656-661). In rvk, whether EXEC succeeds also depends on whether another client's read or the cron happened to touch the stale key.
failure_scenario: Run `SET x foo PX 1`, wait 2 ms, then `WATCH x`. Then `EXISTS x` returns 0: its lazy expiry deletes x and sets the flag. Then `MULTI`, `PING`, `EXEC`. rvk returns a nil array; Valkey returns [PONG]. 'Delete WATCHed stale keys should not fail EXEC' and 'FLUSHDB while watching stale keys should not fail EXEC' (tests/unit/multi.tcl:286, 300) fail. Without the EXISTS, the outcome depends on whether the cron of the thread that owns x's shard ran in between.
suggested_fix: Record at WATCH time whether the key was logically expired. Register stale keys so that removal of an expired entry does not set the flag. Alternatively, keep a per-registration expired bit that is cleared instead of setting the flag when the stale key is deleted.
verifier_reasoning: remove_at always calls notify_watchers_at (store.rs:254), including for lazy expiry in lookup (store.rs:173-174) and cron expire_due (store.rs:324). cmd_watch does not record whether the key was already stale (cmd.rs:1622-1635). Valkey records wk->expired = keyIsExpired at WATCH time (multi.c:526). touchWatchedKey then clears that marker and skips the client when the stale key is deleted (multi.c:609-615), and touchAllWatchedKeysInDb does the same (multi.c:656-661). So SET x foo PX 1, wait 2 ms, WATCH x, EXISTS x (or DEL x), MULTI, PING, EXEC returns a nil array in rvk and [PONG] in Valkey.

title: CONFIG RESETSTAT wipes counters of commands processed after the reset
description: RESETSTAT zeroes the calling thread's counters immediately and bumps reset_epoch (cmd.rs:1908-1911). Each worker, including the caller, compares the epoch with its local seen_reset only after it has processed its whole event batch (server.rs:248-252), and then zeroes its counters again. The calling thread never updates seen_reset when it resets itself. Counts for commands executed after RESETSTAT on the same pipeline, or on other threads before their loop-end check, are erased.
failure_scenario: One write carries pipelined `CONFIG RESETSTAT` and `GET missing`. Both run in the same on_readable, then the loop-end epoch check resets the counters again. A following `INFO stats` reports keyspace_misses:0, and total_commands_processed leaves out the GET. Valkey reports keyspace_misses:1. Across threads, a worker idle in poll wakes for a client's command after RESETSTAT was acknowledged, counts it, and then wipes it.
suggested_fix: Have the calling thread set its seen_reset to the new epoch, e.g. by keeping it in ThreadCtx. Also apply the reset on other threads before processing events (check the epoch right after poll returns), or implement the reset as baseline snapshots taken at reset time.
verifier_reasoning: CONFIG RESETSTAT bumps reset_epoch and resets the caller's stats immediately (cmd.rs:1907-1912). It does not update the worker-local seen_reset, which lives in worker() (server.rs:212). Commands pipelined after it in the same read run in the same process() call and add to shared.stats[id] (for example, misses through cx.hit). After the event batch, the loop sees epoch != seen_reset and calls shared.stats[id].reset() again (server.rs:248-252). That erases the GET's command and miss counts and the net_in/net_out of that batch. A later INFO stats reports keyspace_misses:0, while Valkey would report 1. The same applies to other connections handled later in the same batch, and to other threads that process commands after the RESETSTAT reply but before their loop-end check.

title: maxclients check-then-increment race admits more than maxclients connections
description: Each worker accepts on its own SO_REUSEPORT listener. It reads `shared.connected` (server.rs:274) and increments it later with a separate fetch_add (server.rs:287). Concurrent accepts on different workers can all pass the check.
failure_scenario: With --threads 4 --maxclients 100 and 99 clients connected, four clients connect at once and land on four workers. Each worker sees connected=99 < 100 and accepts, giving 103 connections instead of 100. Valkey rejects the extra three with '-ERR max number of clients reached'.
suggested_fix: Reserve the slot atomically: `if shared.connected.fetch_add(1) >= maxclients { fetch_sub(1); reject }`, and release the reservation on the register-failure path.
verifier_reasoning: accept_all reads shared.connected with a Relaxed load and compares it to maxclients (server.rs:274). It increments with a separate fetch_add only after poll.registry().register, an epoll_ctl syscall (server.rs:283-287). Each worker has its own SO_REUSEPORT listener (server.rs:155, 202-205), so concurrent accepts on different workers can all pass the check at connected=99 and push the count past maxclients. Valkey admits connections on a single thread, so the count cannot overshoot. This is a real TOCTOU race; its impact is small.

title: evict_one: an expired pool candidate is removed without publishing memory or counting it, and a live key is evicted as well
description: In the LRU path, `g.delete(...)` goes through lookup. A candidate that has expired since it was sampled is removed via remove_at, so shard mem drops and watchers are notified, but delete returns false. That branch skips publish_mem (cmd.rs:583) and throws away fx, so expired_keys is not incremented. The loop then pops the next candidate and evicts a live key, even though memory was already freed. The shard's published mem stays too high until the next publish on that shard (up to one cron tick), which inflates used_memory for all threads' make_room decisions.
failure_scenario: Use allkeys-lru with short-TTL keys. Pool candidate K (high idle) expires before it is popped. make_room pops K: K is deleted as expired, not published and not counted in expired_keys. Then the next pool entry J, a live key, is evicted and evicted_keys goes up by 1. Under steady pressure this repeats for each stale candidate: extra live keys are evicted, and INFO expired_keys under-reports.
suggested_fix: Publish mem after every delete attempt. Add fx.expired to the expired stat. If the delete removed an expired entry, count it as progress (return true) instead of evicting another live key.
verifier_reasoning: In evict_one's LRU path, g.delete goes through Shard::lookup (store.rs:280-281). If the pooled candidate's TTL has passed, lookup calls remove_at and increments fx.expired, then returns None, so delete returns false (store.rs:172-176). The caller's fx is a local that is never read (cmd.rs:581), and publish_mem runs only on the true branch (cmd.rs:582-584). The loop then pops the next pool entry and deletes it if it is live, returning true. One evict_one call therefore removes two keys but counts only one eviction and no expiry. If the second key is in a different shard, the first shard's freed memory stays unpublished until the next finish() or cron on that shard, which inflates used_memory for every thread's make_room. Valkey's pool loop evicts a found but logically expired key as the pick (one key, counted in evicted_keys) and does not delete a second one.

title: MULTI/EXEC bypasses maxmemory: DENYOOM commands are neither OOM-checked when queued nor when EXEC runs
description: This is outside the I/O dimension but sits on the same dispatch path. In run_command, a command inside MULTI is queued and returns at lines 415-418, before the DENYOOM/make_room check at line 421. EXEC has no DENYOOM flag, so make_room is skipped for EXEC too. exec_transaction (lines 1591-1611) then calls spec.run on every queued command directly and never calls make_room. In Valkey, processCommand runs performEvictions and rejects DENYOOM commands before queueing (server.c ~4869-4889). It also treats EXEC as DENYOOM when the queue holds a DENYOOM command (combined_flags = cmd_flags | mstate->cmd_flags, server.c:4723-4731).
failure_scenario: Start with --maxmemory 64mb --maxmemory-policy noeviction and fill memory until a plain `SET k v` returns `-OOM command not allowed...`. Then send MULTI, followed by 100 x `SET big:<i> <1MB value>`, then EXEC. rvk replies QUEUED to each SET and EXEC returns 100 x +OK, storing about 100MB beyond maxmemory. Valkey replies -OOM to each queued SET, flags the transaction and EXEC returns -EXECABORT. Under noeviction this works every time, so the memory limit can be exceeded without bound by anyone who wraps writes in MULTI/EXEC.
suggested_fix: Move the DENYOOM/make_room check ahead of the MULTI queueing branch and flag the transaction when it fails. Also record in Multi whether any queued command is DENYOOM, and call make_room before EXEC when one is.
verifier_reasoning: I traced the path. In run_command (cmd.rs:408-419), when conn.multi is Some, every command other than exec/discard/quit/reset is pushed to m.queued and answered QUEUED before the DENYOOM/make_room check at line 421. EXEC is registered with NOMULTI only (line 204), not DENYOOM, so make_room is also skipped for EXEC. exec_transaction (1539-1620) calls spec.run directly and never calls make_room. In Valkey, processCommand ORs mstate->cmd_flags into combined_flags for EXEC (server.c:4723-4731) and calls performEvictions before queueing (server.c:4869; queueMultiCommand is at 5025). On EVICT_FAIL it calls rejectCommand for DENYOOM commands, and rejectCommand calls flagTransaction (server.c:4441), so a later EXEC returns EXECABORT. Under noeviction, the reporter's sequence (MULTI, N large SETs, EXEC) succeeds in rvk at any memory level, so maxmemory can be exceeded without bound.

title: Incomplete multibulk is re-parsed from byte 0 on every readable event (quadratic CPU; one client can pin a worker)
description: resp::parse keeps no state between calls. It clears `ranges` (line 101), and server::process calls it at pos 0 of the retained partial request on every on_readable (server.rs:384). The loop at lines 131-164 walks every bulk header that has already arrived (memchr for CR, parse_i64, ranges.push) before it returns Incomplete. Valkey's parseMultibulk keeps multibulklen, bulklen and argv on the client across reads (networking.c ~4120-4300), so each byte is parsed once. tc.ranges is also never shrunk after such a command: ThreadCtx reuses it for the life of the thread. Its capacity stays in jemalloc 'allocated', and used_memory() reads that value.
failure_scenario:
This needs no requirepass (the default) or an authenticated client. Send `*2147483647
`, then about 100M x `$1
x
` (about 700MB, under the 1GB query-buffer limit), then 1 byte per TCP segment. Each segment causes another full pass over about 100M headers (on the order of a second). The worker thread stays at 100% CPU, and every other connection that SO_REUSEPORT hashed to that worker stalls for seconds per request. Afterwards tc.ranges keeps about 1.2GB (12 bytes x 100M), which inflates used_memory permanently. With maxmemory set, the next writes then trigger eviction or OOM. A legitimate case is a large MSET/DEL with 1M keys over a slow link, which also pegs the worker.
suggested_fix: Keep the parse cursor per connection (args already parsed, byte offset of the next header, and the expected count), and resume from it on the next call instead of starting again from pos. Shrink tc.ranges back to a small capacity after an unusually large command.
verifier_reasoning: resp::parse keeps no state. It clears ranges (resp.rs:101) and re-walks every bulk header from the request start (loop at 131-164) before it returns Incomplete at line 157 or 136. server::process calls it at pos 0 of the retained partial request every time on_readable runs (server.rs:375-385). on_readable runs on every readable edge after draining to a short read. Total parse work is therefore roughly (bytes received so far) times (number of read events), which is quadratic for one large multibulk. Valkey's processMultibulkBuffer keeps c->multibulklen and c->bulklen and advances qb_pos (networking.c ~4185-4220), so each byte is parsed once. tc.ranges is moved back into ThreadCtx after each call (server.rs:402) and is never shrunk anywhere. A 100M-argument request therefore leaves about 1.2-1.6GB of capacity in the thread for good, and jemalloc 'allocated' counts it (read by cron for used_memory when maxmemory > 0). An authenticated client, or any client when requirepass is unset, can trigger this.

title: EOF is missed when FIN arrives with the last data: short-read early exit ignores is_read_closed (connection leak, half-close clients hang)
description: The worker calls on_readable when `ev.is_readable() || ev.is_read_closed()` (line 226) but does not pass the read-closed bit in. on_readable stops at the first short read (`if n < avail { break; }`, lines 333-335) and never issues the read that would return 0. With mio's edge-triggered EPOLLIN|EPOLLRDHUP registration, a FIN that is already queued behind the data raises no new edge. So when data and FIN are delivered in the same wakeup, EOF is never seen. update_interest only issues EPOLL_CTL_MOD when a write blocked, so in the common case nothing re-polls the socket. Valkey's ae is level-triggered and reads again, gets 0 and frees the client.
failure_scenario:
(a) Half-close: `printf 'PING
' | nc -N 127.0.0.1 6379`, or a Python client that calls send then shutdown(SHUT_WR) and reads until EOF. rvk replies +PONG but never closes, so the client waits forever. Valkey closes right after the reply. (b) A client crashes or is killed mid-request (for example after sending `*2
$3
GET
`) and its FIN arrives with that data. No reply is produced, so no RST comes back, and the socket stays in CLOSE_WAIT forever. It counts toward connected_clients and maxclients, and on_disconnect never runs, so its WATCH entries are never removed. Repeated occurrences reach maxclients, and every new client is then refused.
suggested_fix: Pass ev.is_read_closed() into on_readable and, when it is set, keep reading until Ok(0) or WouldBlock. On Ok(0), process what is buffered, flush best-effort, then close.
verifier_reasoning: mio always registers with EPOLLET, and READABLE maps to EPOLLIN|EPOLLRDHUP. The worker calls on_readable on is_read_closed (server.rs:226) but does not pass that bit in. on_readable breaks on the first short read (333-335) and never issues the read that would return 0. Line 232 only closes on is_error, or on is_write_closed (EPOLLHUP) while output is pending. A peer half-close raises EPOLLRDHUP only, so neither branch fires. update_interest re-registers only when write interest changes. If the data and the FIN are both queued before epoll_wait collects the event, no further edge arrives. Two cases follow. (a) A half-closing client (send then SHUT_WR) gets its reply but the server never closes the socket. (b) A client that dies after sending a partial request gets no reply and no RST, so the socket stays in CLOSE_WAIT forever. It keeps its connected/maxclients slot, and on_disconnect/unwatch_all never runs. This depends on timing, but it happens whenever the worker is busy or not yet scheduled when the FIN arrives. Valkey's level-triggered ae reads again, gets 0 and frees the client.

title: Output 'backpressure' keeps reading: input piles up to client-query-buffer-limit (and rbuf doubles to ~2GB), then the client is dropped
description: When wbuf exceeds OUTPUT_PAUSE (64MB), process() only stops executing commands (lines 380-383). READABLE stays registered, and on_readable still drains the socket on every edge, doubling rbuf until rlen exceeds client_query_buffer_limit (line 330), then closes the connection. FEATURE_MATRIX.md (Protocol section, 'Output backpressure') says such a client 'stops being read until it drains', but the code does not do that. Back-pressure never reaches TCP flow control. rbuf.resize(len*2, 0) (line 322) zero-fills, so pages are committed. A connection can hold up to about 2GB of rbuf plus 64MB of wbuf before it is cut.
failure_scenario: A client sends 1.1GB of pipelined `GET bigkey` / `SET` commands (replies over 64MB) before reading any reply, as a write-everything-then-read loader does. Valkey executes everything and buffers the output (normal clients have no output limit by default), and the client then reads every reply. rvk stops executing after about 64MB of replies, buffers the remaining input, and closes the socket once rlen passes 1GB. Commands after the pause point are lost silently and the client gets ECONNRESET. Ten such clients make rvk commit about 20GB.
suggested_fix: While paused, stop reading: skip the read in on_readable, or re-register without READABLE. Resume reading and processing when wbuf drains (on_writable already resumes processing). Alternatively, correct the FEATURE_MATRIX claim and cap rbuf growth.
verifier_reasoning: When wbuf exceeds OUTPUT_PAUSE, process() only returns early (server.rs:380-383). READABLE stays registered (update_interest only adds or removes WRITABLE), and on_readable keeps draining the socket on every edge. rbuf doubles (line 322, zero-filled) until rlen exceeds client_query_buffer_limit, and then the connection is closed (330-331). This contradicts FEATURE_MATRIX.md:41, which says such a client 'stops being read until it drains'. Valkey keeps processing and buffers output (normal clients have no limit by default), so the reporter's write-everything-then-read client completes on Valkey but gets reset on rvk. title: MULTI queue is unbounded: queued argv is not counted against client-query-buffer-limit
description: Each queued command is copied into Multi.queued (`m.queued.push(argv...to_vec())`) with no size accounting. The only limit on the connection is rlen > client_query_buffer_limit in on_readable, which covers raw unparsed bytes only. Valkey counts queued transaction memory as query buffer: qb_memory = sdslen(querybuf) + mstate->argv_len_sums > client_max_querybuf_len closes the client (networking.c ~4795-4804, multi.c:135).
failure_scenario: MULTI, then send `SET k <512MB value>` over and over (each one is a valid bulk at the default proto-max-bulk-len). Valkey disconnects the client once queued memory plus query buffer passes 1GB. rvk stores every value in the queue until the host OOM-kills the process, and all data is lost (no persistence). Before that, with maxmemory and allkeys-lru, the jemalloc 'allocated' figure that make_room reads includes the queue, so other clients' keys are evicted to make room for the uncommitted transaction.
suggested_fix: Track the sum of queued argv bytes in Multi. Add it to rlen when checking client_query_buffer_limit (or check it at queue time), and close the client like Valkey does.

It covers only unparsed bytes in rbuf, and rbuf is compacted and shrunk after each command (server.rs:404-411). Valkey adds mstate->argv_len_sums to the query-buffer size (networking.c:4800-4803; argv_len_sums is incremented in multi.c:135) and disconnects once the total passes client_max_querybuf_len. So in rvk, MULTI followed by repeated large SETs grows memory without bound until the host OOM-kills the process. With maxmemory and an eviction policy, the queue's memory is counted in the jemalloc 'allocated' figure that used_memory reads, so other clients' keys get evicted. The client must be authenticated (or requirepass unset).

title: SHUTDOWN accepts any arguments (including ABORT), runs inside MULTI, and replies +OK
description: SHUTDOWN is registered with arity -1 and flags 0 (line 221). cmd_shutdown ignores its arguments, sets shutdown_requested and close_after_reply, and replies +OK. Valkey's shutdownCommand (db.c:1473-1537) parses NOSAVE/SAVE/NOW/FORCE/ABORT/SAFE/FAILOVER and returns a syntax error for anything else. `SHUTDOWN ABORT` with no shutdown pending returns `-ERR No shutdown in progress.` and does not exit. A successful SHUTDOWN exits without a reply. SHUTDOWN is also NO_MULTI in Valkey (commands/shutdown.json), which contradicts FEATURE_MATRIX's claim that 'Commands Valkey refuses inside MULTI' are verified.

Valkey returns an error and keeps running, but rvk exits the process and all data is lost. `MULTI; SHUTDOWN; EXEC` is queued and kills the server, while Valkey refuses it at queue time. redis-py's `shutdown()` expects a ConnectionError and raises 'SHUTDOWN seems to have failed.' when it gets rvk's +OK.

Severity is low because it is an administrative command, but the behavior on ABORT is the opposite of what was asked.

title: Accept errors (EMFILE/ENFILE) strand the edge-triggered listener backlog; maxclients is never reconciled with RLIMIT_NOFILE
description: accept_all returns on any error other than WouldBlock/Interrupted (`Err(_) => return`). The listener is edge-triggered (mio), so connections still in the kernel accept queue raise no new edge. They are only retried when a new connection arrives. rvk also never adjusts maxclients to the file-descriptor limit. Valkey's adjustOpenFilesLimit lowers maxclients so extra clients get '-ERR max number of clients reached'. With the default maxclients 10000 and a typical soft ulimit of 1024, accept() fails with EMFILE long before maxclients is reached.
failure_scenario: Run under `ulimit -n 1024` and open 1100 connections at once (for example a load generator with -c 1100). The kernel completes the handshake for all of them, but about 80 are never accepted and those clients hang with no error. When other clients later disconnect and free descriptors, the stranded connections are still not accepted until a new connection happens to arrive. In a benchmark this shows up as timeouts or stalled clients, not as clean rejections.
suggested_fix: On startup, raise RLIMIT_NOFILE or clamp maxclients to (limit - reserve) as Valkey does. On EMFILE/ENFILE, keep a reserve fd to accept-and-close, or retry accept from the cron tick so the backlog drains once fds are free.

The mio listener is edge-triggered, so connections still in the kernel accept queue raise no new event until another connection arrives. Freeing descriptors (close_conn) does not wake the listener. rvk has no RLIMIT_NOFILE handling (grep finds no rlimit or nofile in src), and the default maxclients is 10000 (main.rs:53). Valkey's adjustOpenFilesLimit (server.c:2710+) raises the soft limit to maxclients+32 when the hard limit allows. Otherwise it lowers maxclients so that extra clients get an explicit error. Its level-triggered accept also retries as soon as descriptors free up. With the common default soft limit of 1024 and more than about 1000 concurrent clients, rvk leaves the extra connections hanging silently, while Valkey either accepts them all after raising the limit or rejects them cleanly.

title: EOF after a read that exactly filled rbuf closes the connection without executing the buffered commands
description: In on_readable's loop, a read that fills the remaining space (n == avail) continues the loop. If the next read returns Ok(0), the function returns true immediately (line 326), and process_and_flush never runs on bytes already read in the same call. Valkey processes each read before the next one, so commands sent before the FIN are executed.
failure_scenario: On a fresh connection, a client writes exactly 16384 bytes of commands (for example 512 x a 32-byte `SET` line) and then calls shutdown(SHUT_WR) or close(). If both arrive before the worker wakes, the first read returns 16384 (== avail) and the second returns 0, so the connection closes and none of the 512 SETs is applied. Valkey applies all of them. The same happens whenever the final segment exactly fills the remaining buffer space.
suggested_fix: On Ok(0), break out of the read loop with an eof flag, run process() over the buffered input (best-effort flush), then return true.
verifier_reasoning: In on_readable, a read with n == avail continues the loop (333-335 do not break). If the next read returns Ok(0), line 326 returns true right away, and close_conn runs without process_and_flush on the bytes read earlier in the same call. Example: on a fresh connection rbuf is 16384 bytes. The client sends exactly 16384 bytes and then FIN. The first read returns 16384, the buffer grows, the second read returns 0, and the connection closes without executing anything. Valkey processes each read before the next one, so the commands run. Severity is low because the data must end exactly on the buffer boundary.

title: HELLO inside MULTI does not change the framing of later replies in the same EXEC
description: exec_transaction captures `resp3 = conn.resp3` once (line 1589) and builds every queued command's Reply with that value (line 1601). The block meant to handle a protocol switch (lines 1614-1616) is empty. HELLO is allowed in MULTI in Valkey (hello.json has no NO_MULTI), and Valkey's addReply* reads c->resp per reply, so replies after a queued HELLO use the new protocol.
failure_scenario:
On a RESP2 connection: MULTI; HELLO 3; GET missing; EXEC. Valkey returns `*2`, a `%7` map, then `_
`. rvk returns the `%7` map followed by `$-1
`. In the reverse case (RESP3 connection: MULTI; HELLO 2; GET missing; EXEC), rvk sends `_
` to a client that just switched to RESP2, and RESP2-only parsers report a protocol error.
suggested_fix: After each queued command, re-read cx.conn.resp3 and use it for the next Reply (fill in the empty if-block).

The block that checks for a protocol change (1614-1616) is empty. cmd_hello updates only cx.conn.resp3 and that Cx's own r.resp3, so its own reply is a %7 map, but later commands in the same EXEC still use the old protocol. hello.json has no NO_MULTI flag, so Valkey queues HELLO, and later replies follow the new c->resp. On RESP2, 'MULTI; HELLO 3; GET missing; EXEC' produces `$-1` from rvk where Valkey sends `_`. The reverse case sends `_` to a client that has just switched to RESP2.

title: client-query-buffer-limit is checked against raw drained bytes before any are processed, so small limits disconnect normal pipelines
description: on_readable drains the whole socket receive queue (up to tcp_rmem, several MB) into rbuf and checks rlen > client_query_buffer_limit before process() consumes anything. Valkey reads about 16KB (PROTO_IOBUF_LEN) per read and parses between reads, so its querybuf holds only unparsed bytes. Its limit (minimum 1MB) is not reached by a stream of small complete commands.
failure_scenario: Run with --client-query-buffer-limit 1mb, which Valkey accepts (minimum 1MB) and its tests use. A client pipelines 3MB of `SET k:i v` while the worker is briefly busy. rvk reads more than 1MB in one drain and closes the connection with no error reply, losing the batch. Valkey processes the batch without error.
suggested_fix: Run process() between reads (or cap a single drain at the limit) and apply the limit to unconsumed bytes after parsing, plus queued MULTI memory as Valkey does.
verifier_reasoning: on_readable drains the socket until a short read, doubling rbuf, and checks rlen > client_query_buffer_limit after each read, before process() consumes anything (server.rs:318-342). Valkey's config minimum is 1MB (config.c:3669). Valkey reads about 16KB per event and parses before the next read, and its limit check counts only the remaining querybuf plus queued MULTI argv (networking.c:4800). With --client-query-buffer-limit 1mb and more than 1MB of small pipelined commands already in the socket (loopback rmem autotunes to several MB), rvk closes the connection with no error reply and no commands executed, while Valkey processes them all. This only happens with a non-default small limit, so severity is low.

title: SO_REUSEPORT lets a second rvk-server bind the same port silently and split traffic
description: Every listener sets SO_REUSEPORT. Linux lets any other process run by the same user bind the same addr:port if it also sets SO_REUSEPORT, and then load-balances new connections across all listeners in both processes. Valkey does not set SO_REUSEPORT, so a second instance fails with EADDRINUSE.
failure_scenario: A harness run leaves an rvk-server on 6379 (for example after a crash between start and stop). The next run starts rvk-server on 6379 with different maxmemory or threads settings. The bind succeeds, wait_ping passes, and connections are split by 4-tuple hash between the stale process (old data and config) and the new one. A client SETs a key on one connection and GETs nil on another, and benchmark numbers mix the two servers.
suggested_fix: Before binding the reuseport group, bind-probe the port without SO_REUSEPORT (or take a pidfile/flock on the port) and fail start-up if it is in use.
verifier_reasoning: make_listener sets SO_REUSEPORT on every listener (server.rs:145). On Linux, a second process with the same effective UID that also sets SO_REUSEPORT can bind the same addr:port, and the kernel then spreads new connections across both processes. Valkey's anet sets only SO_REUSEADDR (anet.c:388), so a second instance fails with EADDRINUSE. A stale rvk-server would therefore silently share 6379 with a fresh one, splitting keyspace and benchmark traffic. This is an operational hazard rather than a protocol bug, so severity is low.

title: maxclients can be exceeded by up to threads-1 (check and increment are not atomic across workers)
description: Each worker accepts on its own SO_REUSEPORT listener and admits a connection when `connected.load() < maxclients`. The fetch_add happens later (line 287), so workers that accept at the same moment all see the same count.
failure_scenario: With --threads 4 --maxclients 100 and 99 connected, a burst of 4 connects hashed to the 4 workers can all read 99 and all be admitted, giving 103 clients where Valkey admits exactly 100 and rejects the rest.
suggested_fix: Reserve a slot with fetch_add first, and if the result is >= maxclients, fetch_sub and reject.
verifier_reasoning: Each worker accepts on its own SO_REUSEPORT listener and admits a connection after a relaxed load of connected < maxclients (server.rs:274). The fetch_add happens later (287), so the check and the increment are not atomic across threads. Workers that accept at the same moment can all see maxclients-1 and all admit, overshooting maxclients by up to threads-1. Valkey accepts on a single thread, so its count is exact. The impact is small.

title: Protocol-error replies are written unsanitized (raw CR/LF or UTF-8-expanded byte in the error line)
description: process() writes Parsed::Error text directly into wbuf instead of using Reply::error, which replaces CR and LF. resp.rs:142 builds `got '{}'` from `buf[p] as char`. So a raw '\n' or '\r' byte goes into the error line, and a byte >= 0x80 becomes a 2-byte UTF-8 sequence. Valkey's addReplyErrorFormat maps \r and \n to spaces and prints the raw byte with %c.
failure_scenario:
Input `*1


`. rvk replies `-ERR Protocol error: expected '$', got '
'
` with an embedded LF. Valkey replies `... got ' '`. Input `*1
\xff
` gives `got 'Ã¿'` (C3 BF) in rvk and the single byte 0xFF in Valkey. Exact-match comparisons such as the differential test mismatch, and line-based readers see a split error line.
suggested_fix: Write protocol errors through Reply::error (with resp3 irrelevant), and format the byte as a raw u8, not as a char.

process() appends Parsed::Error text to wbuf directly (server.rs:392-396) and skips Reply::error's CR/LF replacement. resp.rs:142 formats buf[p] as char, so 0x0A is emitted raw and bytes >= 0x80 become 2-byte UTF-8. For `*1


`, Valkey takes the same path (networking.c:4213-4215 returns MBULK_UNEXPECTED_CHARACTER, then 3632 uses %c). addReplyErrorFormatInternal maps  and 
 to spaces (networking.c:1066-1069), and %c emits the raw byte. So rvk's error line contains an embedded LF or C3 BF where Valkey sends a space or 0xFF. The connection closes right after, so the impact is cosmetic or framing only.

title: u32 argument offsets truncate when proto-max-bulk-len / client-query-buffer-limit exceed 4GB (wrong argument or worker panic)
description: ArgRange stores start and end as u32 (`start as u32`, `end as u32`) as absolute offsets into rbuf. main.rs accepts any size for --proto-max-bulk-len and --client-query-buffer-limit (lines 77-79) with no upper bound, and Valkey allows both up to LONG_MAX. If rbuf grows past 4GiB, the offsets wrap.
failure_scenario: Run with --proto-max-bulk-len 5gb --client-query-buffer-limit 8gb, then `SET k <4.5GB value>`. end wraps modulo 2^32 to below start, so Args::get slices `s[start..end]` with end < start and panics. That worker thread dies with all its connections, and main panics at join. With other sizes the wrapped range is still valid and SET silently stores the wrong bytes.
suggested_fix: Use usize offsets in ArgRange, or reject configs above u32::MAX at start-up.
verifier_reasoning: ArgRange stores absolute rbuf offsets as u32 (resp.rs:25-26, cast at 162), while length checks use usize. main.rs parse_memory places no upper bound on --proto-max-bulk-len or --client-query-buffer-limit, and Valkey allows both up to LONG_MAX (config.c:3648, 3669). Nothing in cmd.rs caps value size. One correction to the report: for the given example (a 4.5GiB value starting at offset ~13), end wraps to about 512MiB, which is still greater than start. So no panic occurs, and SET silently stores a 512MiB prefix (wrong data). A panic needs start <= u32::MAX < end with wrapped end < start. Also, the workspace profile has panic = "abort" (poc/Cargo.toml:19), so such a panic aborts the whole process rather than one worker. The defect needs non-default configs above 4GiB, hence low.

title: No TCP keepalive on accepted sockets, so dead peers are never reaped
description: accept_all sets only TCP_NODELAY. Valkey enables keepalive on every accepted socket by default (tcp-keepalive 300, config.c:3574; socket.c:349). rvk also has no idle timeout, so a peer that disappears without FIN or RST keeps its slot forever.
failure_scenario: A client host loses power, or a NAT drops state, while its connection is idle. Valkey's keepalive probes fail after a few minutes and the client is freed. rvk keeps the fd, the 32KB of buffers and the maxclients slot indefinitely. Over repeated events connected_clients climbs until new clients get '-ERR max number of clients reached'.
suggested_fix: Enable SO_KEEPALIVE with a 300s idle time (socket2 TcpKeepalive) on accepted sockets, as Valkey's default does.
verifier_reasoning: accept_all sets only TCP_NODELAY (server.rs:272), and the rvk source contains no keepalive or idle-timeout code (grep finds none). Valkey defaults tcp-keepalive to 300 (config.c:3574) and enables it on every accepted socket (socket.c:349). A peer that disappears while idle without sending FIN or RST is therefore reaped by Valkey after the keepalive probes fail, but rvk holds its fd, buffers and maxclients slot indefinitely. Severity is low because it needs network partitions or host failures to build up.

title: INFO or UNWATCH queued inside MULTI deadlocks the worker thread at EXEC
description: exec_transaction (cmd.rs:1556-1580) locks the shard of every watched key and every key in the queued commands, then runs the queued commands while those guards are still held. Two queued commands lock shards themselves, outside the Cx lock set. cmd_info runs `sh.store.lock(i)` for every shard (1957-1961). cmd_unwatch calls unwatch_all (108-114), which runs `store.lock(shard_of(key))` for each watched key. Both locks are std::sync::Mutex, which is not reentrant, so the second lock on a shard the same thread already holds blocks forever. Valkey allows both commands inside MULTI: INFO has no NO_MULTI flag, and unwatch.json has none either. Valkey's execCommand unwatches before it runs the queue.
failure_scenario: `WATCH k` / `MULTI` / `UNWATCH` / `EXEC`: the shard of k is locked for EXEC, then unwatch_all tries to lock it again and the worker hangs. Likewise `MULTI` / `SET k v` / `INFO` / `EXEC`, or `MULTI` / `DBSIZE` / `INFO` / `EXEC` (all 64 shards held). The hung worker keeps holding those shard locks, so every other worker that touches those shards also blocks. The whole server stops responding and no error is ever returned.
suggested_fix: In exec_transaction, unwatch before running the queue (as Valkey does) and make cmd_unwatch a no-op inside EXEC. Have cmd_info read key counts through the already-held guards when it runs inside EXEC, or read them lock-free from per-shard atomics as is already done for mem.
verifier_reasoning: Traced end to end. exec_transaction (cmd.rs:1556-1580) puts the shard of every watched key into `ids` and holds all of those guards in `locks` while it runs the queue (1590-1617). UNWATCH (flags 0, Keys::None) and INFO (flags 0) pass the NOMULTI check at 409 and are queued at 415-418. At EXEC, cmd_unwatch calls unwatch_all (108-114), which calls store.lock(shard_of(key)) on a shard this thread already holds. cmd_info calls sh.store.lock(i) for i in 0..64 (1957-1961), so it blocks on the first shard already in `locks`. Store::lock is std::sync::Mutex::lock().unwrap() (store.rs:112). The futex Mutex has no owner tracking, so a second lock from the same thread waits forever. Sequences that hang: `WATCH k / MULTI / UNWATCH / EXEC`, `MULTI / SET k v / INFO / EXEC`, `WATCH k / MULTI / INFO / EXEC`, and `MULTI / DBSIZE / INFO / EXEC` (all 64 shards held). The stuck worker keeps holding its guards, so every other worker that locks those shards also blocks. Valkey allows both commands in MULTI: unwatch.json and info.json have no NO_MULTI, and execCommand calls unwatchAllKeys before it runs the queue (multi.c).

title: MULTI/EXEC bypasses maxmemory: no OOM rejection and no eviction for queued writes
description: In run_command, a command inside MULTI is queued and returns (408-419) before the DENYOOM/make_room check (421). EXEC has no DENYOOM flag, so it skips make_room, and exec_transaction calls spec.run directly with no memory check or eviction. In Valkey, processCommand runs performEvictions before queueing and rejects DENYOOM commands under OOM, which also flags the transaction for EXECABORT. At EXEC it ORs the queued commands' flags (mstate->cmd_flags) and aborts with `EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of: OOM ...`. Valkey's tests/unit/multi.tcl tests 'DISCARD should not fail during OOM' and 'EXEC with at least one use-memory command should fail' check this.
failure_scenario: With maxmemory reached under noeviction, `MULTI` / `SET big <100MB>` / `EXEC` stores the value, where Valkey returns OOM then EXECABORT. Repeating this grows memory without bound. Under allkeys-lru, a client that writes only through transactional pipelines (redis-py `pipeline()` defaults to transaction=True) never triggers eviction, so memory climbs far past maxmemory.
suggested_fix: Run make_room (or a plain OOM check) before queueing a DENYOOM command inside MULTI, and set m.errored on failure. Track an OR of the queued commands' flags and run the OOM check at EXEC, failing with 'EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of: OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.'
