EXEC's spec has only NOMULTI, so make_room is skipped for EXEC. exec_transaction calls spec.run directly (1610), and in_exec is never true, so no path checks memory or evicts for queued writes. cron does not evict either. Valkey's processCommand (server.c ~4718-4731, ~4868-4885) calls performEvictions before every command when maxmemory is set. It ORs mstate->cmd_flags into is_denyoom_command for EXEC and rejects with oomerr. rejectCommand calls flagTransaction, and for EXEC it calls execCommandAbort, which produces EXECABORT. multi.tcl:887 'EXEC with at least one use-memory command should fail' expects EXECABORT*OOM*, but rvk returns [OK, 1]. Under noeviction, transactional SETs succeed above maxmemory without limit. Under allkeys-lru, a client that writes only through MULTI/EXEC never triggers eviction.

title: DEBUG SLEEP inf (or any value of 1e20 or more) panics and, with panic=abort, kills the server; DEBUG is not protected
description: `secs` comes from `str::parse::<f64>`, which accepts "inf" and "1e30". `secs.max(0.0)` leaves those values unchanged, and `Duration::from_secs_f64` panics on infinite values or values that overflow Duration. The workspace release profile sets `panic = "abort"`, so the whole process dies. DEBUG is in the command table with flags 0, so any authenticated client can run it. Valkey marks DEBUG as PROTECTED (refused unless enable-debug-command is set), and its DEBUG SLEEP uses strtod and nanosleep, which do not crash.
failure_scenario: Any client sends `DEBUG SLEEP inf` or `DEBUG SLEEP 1e20`. The worker panics and the process aborts, so all data and connections are lost.
suggested_fix: Reject values that are not finite or are too large (for example with Duration::try_from_secs_f64), and gate DEBUG behind an enable-debug-command style option.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_debug at cmd.rs:2031 parses the argument with str::parse::<f64>. Rust 1.97 accepts "inf" and "infinity" in any case, and accepts "1e20". inf.max(0.0) stays inf. Duration::from_secs_f64 panics when the value is not finite or exceeds u64::MAX seconds (about 1.8e19), so both inputs panic. NaN becomes 0 through max and does not panic. The workspace release profile sets panic = "abort" (poc/Cargo.toml), so the whole process aborts. DEBUG is in the table with flags 0 (cmd.rs:220), so any authenticated client can send it, and any client at all when requirepass is unset. Valkey's debug.json carries PROTECTED, so processCommand refuses DEBUG unless enable-debug-command allows it.

title: WATCH does not follow Valkey's rules for expired keys or for FLUSH of keys that do not exist
description: rvk invalidates a watch only when a shard physically modifies the key (notify_watchers*), and EXEC checks only that flag (cmd.rs:1581). Valkey's rules (multi.c watchForKey, isWatchedKeyExpired, touchWatchedKey, touchAllWatchedKeysInDb) differ in three ways. (a) A key that was live at WATCH time and has logically expired before EXEC makes EXEC fail even if nobody has deleted it yet. rvk has no isWatchedKeyExpired check and commits. (b) A key that was already expired at WATCH time and is later lazily deleted or flushed does not invalidate the watch in Valkey. In rvk, Shard::lookup -> remove_at -> notify_watchers_at sets the flag. (c) FLUSHALL/FLUSHDB invalidate only watches on keys that exist. Shard::clear (store.rs:290-294) notifies every watched key, including keys that do not exist.
failure_scenario: Each of these Valkey tests (tests/unit/multi.tcl) gets the opposite result. 'EXEC fail on lazy expired WATCHed key' (`SET key 1 PX 100`, `WATCH key`, sleep 101 ms, `MULTI`, `INCR key`, `EXEC`): rvk returns [1], Valkey nil. 'Delete WATCHed stale keys should not fail EXEC' (`WATCH x` on an already-expired x, then `EXISTS x`): rvk returns nil, Valkey [PONG]. 'FLUSHDB while watching stale keys' and 'FLUSHALL does not touch non affected keys' (`DEL x`, `WATCH x`, `FLUSHALL`, `MULTI`, `PING`, `EXEC`): rvk returns nil, Valkey [PONG]. In case (a), a compare-and-set commits after the watched value has disappeared.
suggested_fix: Record per watched key whether it was expired at WATCH time. At EXEC, after taking the locks, fail if any key that was not expired at WATCH time has now expired. Do not set the flag when a key that was already expired at WATCH time is deleted. In clear(), notify only watched keys that are present and not expired.
verifier_reasoning: I checked all three sub-claims against multi.c and multi.tcl. (a) Valkey's execCommand calls isWatchedKeyExpired, which skips keys already expired at WATCH time (wk->expired) and sets dirty_cas when a key has expired since. rvk checks only watch_flag (1581). INCR's lazy delete sets the flag only after that check. With active expire off on a 1-thread server, test 'EXEC fail on lazy expired WATCHed key' (multi.tcl:254) gets [1] where Valkey gets nil. (b) cmd_watch never looks the key up, so an already-expired x is registered as a normal watch. EXISTS then reaches Shard::lookup, remove_at and notify_watchers_at, which sets the flag. In Valkey, touchWatchedKey with wk->expired and the key gone clears the expired mark and skips the client. Test multi.tcl:286 gets nil where Valkey gets PONG. (c) Shard::clear (store.rs:290-294) notifies every watched key. Valkey's touchAllWatchedKeysInDb flags only keys that exist, and stale expired keys are skipped. Tests multi.tcl:300 and 361 get nil where Valkey gets PONG.

title: WATCH duplicate check is quadratic and runs while holding shard locks
description: cmd_watch scans the whole `conn.watched` Vec for every key (`iter().any(|k| k == key)`), so WATCH of N keys costs O(N^2). The command holds the locks on every shard its keys hash to (KALL1), which for large N is all 64 shards. Valkey uses a per-client hashtable, so each key is O(1).
failure_scenario: Valkey's own test 'WATCH with large number of keys' runs `WATCH key{t}-0 ... key{t}-49999` twice. Each run is about 1.25e9 byte-slice comparisons while all shards are locked, which stalls every client on every worker for seconds. With 200k keys the stall lasts minutes, and any authenticated client can trigger it.
suggested_fix: Keep a per-connection HashSet of watched keys, or deduplicate per shard through the shard's watched map, which is already keyed by key.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_watch (1626-1635) runs `conn.watched.iter().any(|k| k == key)` for each argument, so one WATCH of N new keys costs about N^2/2 slice comparisons. Repeating WATCH with the same N keys also costs about N^2/2, because key j is found at position j. WATCH is KALL1, so lock_for holds every shard the keys hash to. 50k keys cover all 64 shards. Valkey's watchForKey (multi.c:489-533) checks duplicates with hashtableFind on a per-client per-db hashtable, which is O(1) per key. Valkey's test 'WATCH with large number of keys' (multi.tcl:544) runs WATCH with 50k keys twice. In rvk each run is about 1.25e9 comparisons, mostly 12-byte compares, while every shard is locked, which stalls all other clients for seconds.

title: EXPIRETIME truncates to seconds; Valkey rounds
description: The code comment claims EXPIRETIME reports `ms / 1000`. Valkey's ttlGenericCommand(c, 0, 1) returns `(ttl + 500) / 1000` for EXPIRETIME, the same rounding TTL uses (expire.c:925). rvk returns `exp / 1000`.
failure_scenario: `SET k v` / `PEXPIREAT k 4102444800600` / `EXPIRETIME k`: Valkey returns 4102444801, rvk returns 4102444800. After `SET k v EX 100` or `EXPIRE k 100`, the deadline is now_ms + 100000, so about half of all keys differ by one second.
suggested_fix: Use ttl_generic(cx, false, true) for EXPIRETIME.
verifier_reasoning: expire.c:941 makes expiretimeCommand call ttlGenericCommand(c, 0, 1). For output_ms=0 that function returns (ttl + 500) / 1000 (line 925), with ttl being the absolute expiry. rvk's cmd_expiretime (1298) returns exp / 1000, and the code comment states the opposite of Valkey's behavior. For PEXPIREAT k 4102444800600, Valkey returns 4102444801 and rvk returns 4102444800. Keys whose millisecond part is 500 or more differ by one second. The value is off by at most one second, so I rate it low rather than medium.

title: SHUTDOWN ignores its arguments and is accepted inside MULTI
description: cmd_shutdown shuts down for any argument list, and the table entry (221) lacks NOMULTI. In Valkey, SHUTDOWN parses NOSAVE/SAVE/NOW/FORCE/ABORT/SAFE/FAILOVER and returns a syntax error for anything else. `SHUTDOWN ABORT` cancels a pending shutdown ('No shutdown in progress.' if there is none). shutdown.json carries NO_MULTI.
failure_scenario: An operator sends `SHUTDOWN ABORT` to cancel a shutdown, or makes a typo such as `SHUTDOWN NOSAV`, and rvk terminates the process. `MULTI` / `SHUTDOWN` / `EXEC` is queued and kills the server at EXEC, whereas Valkey rejects it with "Command 'shutdown' not allowed inside a transaction" and EXECABORT.
suggested_fix: Parse the arguments as Valkey does. Make ABORT return 'No shutdown in progress.' and return a syntax error for unknown tokens. Add NOMULTI to the spec.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_shutdown (2055-2059) ignores argv and always sets shutdown_requested. The worker loop then sets shared.shutdown and calls process::exit(0) (server.rs:244-258). The table entry (221) has flags 0, so SHUTDOWN is queued inside MULTI and runs at EXEC. Valkey's shutdown.json has NO_MULTI, which gives "Command 'shutdown' not allowed inside a transaction" and flags the transaction. Valkey's shutdownCommand (db.c:1473-1511) accepts only nosave/save/now/force/abort and returns a syntax error for anything else. SHUTDOWN ABORT returns 'No shutdown in progress.' when nothing is pending. In rvk, SHUTDOWN ABORT or a typo such as SHUTDOWN NOSAV terminates the process.

title: Unauthenticated clients get unknown-command and arity errors instead of NOAUTH
description: run_command does the command lookup (384) and the arity check (392) before the auth check (400). Valkey's processCommand checks authRequired first and sends NOAUTH for any command without NO_AUTH, including unknown commands (`!c->cmd || !(flags & CMD_NO_AUTH)`), so it does not reveal which commands exist before AUTH.
failure_scenario: With requirepass set and no AUTH: `FOOBAR` returns "ERR unknown command 'FOOBAR'..." (Valkey: "NOAUTH Authentication required."), and `GET` with no key returns "ERR wrong number of arguments for 'get' command" (Valkey: NOAUTH). Clients that detect NOAUTH to trigger re-authentication do not see it.
suggested_fix: Do the NOAUTH check before the lookup and arity errors. Treat an unknown command as not NO_AUTH.
verifier_reasoning: run_command does the lookup (384) and the arity check (392) before the auth check (400). Valkey's processCommand (server.c ~4678-4700) checks authRequired first and sends noautherr when `!c->cmd || !(c->cmd->flags & CMD_NO_AUTH)`. It reports existence and arity errors (READ_FLAGS_BAD_ARITY) only after that. With requirepass set and no AUTH, rvk answers FOOBAR with 'unknown command' and a bare GET with an arity error, where Valkey answers NOAUTH to both.

title: Subcommand errors for CLIENT/CONFIG are not caught at queue time and have the wrong text
description: CLIENT, CONFIG, COMMAND and DEBUG are single table entries. Unknown subcommands and subcommand arity errors are detected only inside the handler, so inside MULTI they are QUEUED and the transaction is not marked errored. In Valkey, lookupCommand resolves container subcommands, so processCommand returns 'unknown subcommand' or "wrong number of arguments for 'config|get' command" immediately and calls flagTransaction. rvk's match guards (e.g. `"get" if argc >= 3`, `"set" if argc >= 4 && even`, `("id", 2)`) send arity mistakes into the 'unknown subcommand' branch. CLIENT LIST also lists only the calling connection, and it rejects the TYPE/ID filters that client-list.json (arity -2) allows.
failure_scenario: `MULTI` / `CONFIG GETT x` / `SET k v` / `EXEC`: Valkey returns an error and then EXECABORT, so k is not set. rvk returns QUEUED and EXEC sets k. `CONFIG GET` alone returns "ERR unknown subcommand 'GET'. Try CONFIG HELP." instead of "ERR wrong number of arguments for 'config|get' command". `CLIENT ID x` returns unknown subcommand instead of the client|id arity error. With 50 clients connected, `CLIENT LIST` returns 1 line.
suggested_fix: Give subcommands their own arity table, validate it in run_command before queueing, and set m.errored on failure.
verifier_reasoning: CONFIG (-2), CLIENT (-2), COMMAND and DEBUG are single table entries, so `CONFIG GETT x` passes arity and is QUEUED without setting errored. EXEC then runs the following SET. In Valkey, lookupCommand resolves subcommands. commandCheckExistence (server.c:4518-4528) produces "unknown subcommand '...'. Try CONFIG HELP.", and rejectCommandSds calls flagTransaction, so EXEC returns EXECABORT. rvk's match guards send arity mistakes to the unknown-subcommand branch. `CONFIG GET` alone and `CLIENT ID x` both get 'unknown subcommand', where Valkey reports an arity error for config|get (arity -3) or client|id (arity 2). CLIENT LIST (1789-1799) formats only the caller's own connection and accepts only argc==2, while client-list.json has arity -2 with TYPE/ID filters.

title: RANDOMKEY returns nil while live keys exist when most slots hold expired keys
description: cmd_randomkey samples 100 random slab positions and skips expired entries without deleting them, then returns nil. Valkey's dbRandomKey deletes each expired key it samples and keeps looping on a primary, so it always returns a live key if one exists, and the deletions also reduce later sampling cost.
failure_scenario: With `DEBUG SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE 0` and 1 thread: SET 10000 keys with `PX 1`, SET one persistent key, wait 2 ms, then `RANDOMKEY` returns nil about 99% of the time (1-(10000/10001)^100 is about 1%). Valkey returns the live key. Repeating the call never makes progress because nothing is deleted.
suggested_fix: Remove expired keys as they are sampled (the Many guards are already held), and keep sampling until a live key is found or the store is empty.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_randomkey (1478-1498) takes 100 uniform samples over all slab slots, including expired ones. It skips expired entries without deleting them and returns null after 100 misses. Valkey's dbRandomKey (db.c:462-491) loops until it finds a live key on a primary, deleting each expired key it samples through expireIfNeededWithDictIndex. The maxtries cap applies only to replica, import or paused cases where every key is volatile. With active expire off, 10000 expired keys and 1 live key, rvk returns nil about 99% of the time, and repeated calls make no progress.

title: CONFIG SET is not atomic, and the maxmemory parser overflows silently and rejects Valkey's k/m/g units
description: cmd_config 'set' applies each pair as it goes and returns an error at the first bad pair, leaving earlier pairs applied. Valkey's multi-parameter CONFIG SET is all-or-nothing. crate_parse_memory computes `v * mul` with no overflow check; release builds have no overflow-checks, so the result wraps. It also accepts only gb/mb/kb, while main.rs parse_memory and Valkey's memtoull also accept k/m/g.
failure_scenario: `CONFIG SET maxmemory 100mb maxmemory-policy bogus` returns an error but leaves maxmemory at 100mb (Valkey leaves it unchanged). `CONFIG SET maxmemory 17179869184gb` wraps to 0, which silently disables the memory limit, where Valkey returns an error. `CONFIG SET maxmemory 100m` is refused even though `--maxmemory 100m` is accepted at start-up.
suggested_fix: Validate all pairs before applying any, use checked_mul, and share one parser with main.rs.
verifier_reasoning: Two of the three sub-claims hold. Non-atomic: cmd_config 'set' (1882-1905) stores maxmemory before it validates the next pair. Valkey's configSetCommand (config.c ~984-995) validates everything, sets all values, and on failure calls restoreBackupConfig. Units: crate_parse_memory accepts only gb/mb/kb, so '100m' fails, while main.rs parse_memory and Valkey's memtoull (util.c:258-271) accept k/m/g and b. The overflow sub-claim is REFUTED. Valkey's memtoull also ends in an unchecked `return val * mul;` (util.c:294), so 17179869184gb wraps to 0 in Valkey too, and 0 is inside maxmemory's [0, ULLONG_MAX] range, giving the same silent result.

title: INCRBYFLOAT range and small-value formatting differ from Valkey beyond the documented last-digit difference
description: Valkey computes in long double (range about 1e4932) and formats with "%.17Lf" plus trailing-zero trimming, so values below 1e-17 print as "0". string2ld also rejects underflow (ERANGE with FP_ZERO). rvk uses f64 and Display. FEATURE_MATRIX documents only last-digit differences, but these differences change the whole value or turn a result into an error.
failure_scenario: `INCRBYFLOAT k 1e-20` on a missing key: Valkey returns and stores "0", rvk returns "0.00000000000000000001". `SET k 1e308` / `INCRBYFLOAT k 1e308`: Valkey returns a 309-digit value, rvk returns "ERR increment would produce NaN or Infinity". `INCRBYFLOAT k 1e-5000`: Valkey returns "ERR value is not a valid float", rvk succeeds. `INCRBYFLOAT k 0x10`: Valkey (strtold) returns 16, rvk returns an error.
suggested_fix: Emulate %.17f-with-trimming formatting (round to 17 fractional digits) and document the f64 range limit, or use a software extended-precision type.
verifier_reasoning: Valkey's incrbyfloatCommand works in long double. It parses with string2ld, which uses strtold and rejects ERANGE with FP_ZERO (util.c:745-763), and formats with createStringObjectFromLongDouble in human mode, "%.17Lf" with trailing zeros trimmed (util.c:1032-1046). rvk uses f64 parse and Display (fmt_float, 1039-1049). 1e-20 on a missing key: Valkey returns '0', rvk returns '0.00000000000000000001' because Rust Display never uses an exponent. 1e308+1e308 is finite in 80-bit long double but inf in f64, so rvk errors. Rust parses 1e-5000 as Ok(0.0) where strtold underflows and is rejected. strtold accepts '0x10' but Rust's parse does not.

title: KEYS glob differs from stringmatchlen on unterminated '[' and on Valkey's nesting cutoff
description: For an unterminated character class, Valkey treats the end of the pattern as the end of the class and continues. rvk sets `p = q + 1` past the end of the pattern, so the final `p == pat.len()` check always fails. Valkey's recursive matcher also returns 'no match' once nesting passes 1000 stars, while rvk's iterative matcher has no such cutoff.
failure_scenario: `SET a 1` / `KEYS "[abc"`: Valkey returns [a], rvk returns []. Valkey's keyspace.tcl test 'Regression for pattern matching very long nested loops' (`SET` of a 50000-character 'a' key, `KEYS` of ("*?" x 50000)) expects {}, but rvk returns the key. The same matcher serves CONFIG GET.
suggested_fix: Treat an unterminated class as Valkey does (p = pat.len() after the class), and match the nesting > 1000 cutoff if exact parity is wanted.
verifier_reasoning: I traced pattern "[abc" against key "a" in both matchers. In Valkey's stringmatchlen_impl (util.c:110-163), the patternLen==0 branch backs up one character and breaks with match=1. The outer loop then ends with patternLen==0 and stringLen==0 and returns 1. In rvk's glob_match, the class loop ends at q==pat.len(), p is set to q+1 (5 for a 4-byte pattern), and the final `p == pat.len()` is false, so it does not match. Valkey also returns 0 once nesting > 1000 (util.c:75), so keyspace.tcl:643 expects {}. rvk's iterative matcher matches the 50000-char key, so it returns the key.

title: Read-only lookups refresh the LRU clock and keyspace hit/miss stats are mostly not counted
description: Every command calls Cx::find, which uses touch_lookup and updates `lru`. Valkey's TTL/PTTL/EXPIRETIME/PEXPIRETIME, TYPE and EXISTS use LOOKUP_NOTOUCH. Only GET, GETEX, GETDEL and MGET call cx.hit. Valkey counts keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses for every read lookup, including STRLEN, GETRANGE, EXISTS, TYPE, TTL, GETSET and SET ... GET (via getGenericCommand).
failure_scenario: Under allkeys-lru, a monitor that polls `TTL` or `EXISTS` on keys keeps them looking recently used, so they are never evicted (in Valkey they are). INFO keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses under-count for STRLEN, GETRANGE, EXISTS, TYPE, TTL, GETSET and SET GET, so hit-ratio dashboards differ from Valkey.
suggested_fix: Add a lookup variant that does not touch the LRU clock and use it for TTL*, TYPE and EXISTS. Call cx.hit in the remaining read paths.
verifier_reasoning: Cx::find always calls touch_lookup, which sets slot.lru (store.rs:183-187). The LRU eviction in evict_one ranks candidates by that lru. Valkey uses LOOKUP_NOTOUCH for TTL/PTTL/EXPIRETIME (expire.c:910), EXISTS (db.c ~943) and TYPE (db.c ~1468). Valkey's lookupKey counts keyspace hits and misses for every lookup without LOOKUP_WRITE or NOSTATS (db.c:123-127), which includes STRLEN, GETRANGE, EXISTS, TYPE and TTL, and GETSET and SET...GET through getGenericCommand. rvk calls cx.hit only in GET, GETEX, GETDEL and MGET (cmd.rs 630, 854, 875, 891).

title: Expiry boundary is off by one millisecond (expire <= now versus Valkey's now > expire)
description: Shard::lookup, KEYS (cmd.rs:1457) and RANDOMKEY (1487) treat a key as expired when `exp <= now`. Valkey's timestampIsExpired returns `now > when`, so a key is still live during the millisecond equal to its deadline.
failure_scenario: A key with a PXAT deadline T, read at the millisecond T: Valkey's PTTL returns 0 and GET returns the value, while rvk returns -2 and nil.
suggested_fix: Use `exp < now` for expiry checks during lookup.
verifier_reasoning: Valkey's timestampIsExpired (expire.c:975-982) returns `now > when`. rvk treats a key as expired when `exp <= now`, in Shard::lookup (store.rs:173), KEYS (1457) and RANDOMKEY (1487). At now == T for a PXAT T key, Valkey returns the value and PTTL 0, while rvk deletes the key and returns nil and -2. The divergence lasts one millisecond. SET's already-expired check (`when <= now`) matches Valkey's checkAlreadyExpired, so only reads are affected.

title: HELLO authenticates before validating its other options, and does not validate SETNAME
description: cmd_hello sets `conn.authed = true` as soon as it parses AUTH, then can still return a syntax error for a later option. Valkey parses and validates every option first (including validateClientName for SETNAME) and only then authenticates. rvk also never applies CLIENT SETNAME's character validation to HELLO SETNAME.
failure_scenario: Unauthenticated: `HELLO 3 AUTH default <pw> BOGUS` returns "ERR Syntax error in HELLO option 'BOGUS'", but the connection is now authenticated and still on RESP2. In Valkey it stays unauthenticated. `HELLO 3 SETNAME "a b"` succeeds and stores a name with a space, where Valkey rejects it, and the name breaks the space-separated fields of CLIENT LIST/INFO.
suggested_fix: Collect user, password and name during parsing, validate the name, and set authed only after the loop has completed without error.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_hello sets conn.authed = true inside the option loop (1733), before later options are validated. `HELLO 3 AUTH default <pw> BOGUS` therefore returns the syntax error but leaves the connection authenticated and on RESP2. Valkey's helloCommand (networking.c ~6351-6373) parses every option first, calls validateClientName for SETNAME, and calls ACLAuthenticateUser only after that. rvk applies no character validation to HELLO SETNAME, though CLIENT SETNAME does it at 1782, so `HELLO 3 SETNAME "a b"` is accepted.

title: HELLO inside EXEC does not switch the protocol for later replies in the same EXEC
description: exec_transaction captures `resp3` once (1589) and builds each queued command's Reply with it. The block at 1614-1616 that was meant to handle a protocol change is empty. In Valkey, HELLO changes c->resp immediately, so later replies in the same EXEC use the new protocol.
failure_scenario: `MULTI` / `HELLO 3` / `GET missing` / `EXEC` on a RESP2 connection: Valkey encodes the GET result as RESP3 null `_`, rvk as `$-1`.
suggested_fix: Refresh `resp3` from cx.conn.resp3 after each queued command.
verifier_reasoning: exec_transaction reads `resp3 = conn.resp3` once (1589) and builds every queued command's Reply with that value (1601). cmd_hello updates only conn.resp3 and that one cx.r, and the branch at 1614-1616 is empty. hello.json has no NO_MULTI, so HELLO is queued in both servers. In Valkey c->resp changes immediately, so a later `GET missing` in the same EXEC is encoded as `_` in Valkey and `$-1` in rvk.

title: EXEC with condition arguments is rejected and leaves the client stuck in MULTI
description: In this Valkey tree, EXEC has arity -1 and accepts IFEQ/IFNE/NX/XX conditions (multi.c checkExecConditions). rvk declares arity 1. Inside MULTI, the arity error path sets m.errored and returns without ending the transaction.
failure_scenario: `MULTI` / `SET d x` / `EXEC NX cond`: Valkey runs the transaction if cond is absent. rvk returns "ERR wrong number of arguments for 'exec' command" and the connection stays in MULTI, so later commands reply QUEUED and the next plain EXEC returns EXECABORT.
suggested_fix: Implement EXEC conditions, or at least end the MULTI state when EXEC fails its arity check.
verifier_reasoning: In this tree exec.json has arity -1 with the history note 'Added the IFEQ, IFNE, NX, and XX options' (9.2.0). multi.c:206-310 parses and evaluates these conditions in parseExecCondition and checkExecConditions. rvk declares EXEC with arity 1 (204). In MULTI, `EXEC NX cond` fails the arity check at 392, which sets m.errored and returns without clearing conn.multi. Later commands are QUEUED and the next plain EXEC returns EXECABORT. Valkey runs the transaction when cond is absent.

title: APPEND and SETRANGE copy the whole value on every call (quadratic growth)
description: cmd_append copies the existing value with `to_vec()`, extends it, and replace_value copies key and value into a new Box. cmd_setrange copies the whole value twice even to change one byte. Valkey grows the sds in place with sdsMakeRoomFor, so appends are amortized O(len(append)) and SETRANGE is O(len(value argument)).
failure_scenario: Building a 100 MB value with 1 KB `APPEND` calls copies about 5e12 bytes in rvk versus about 1e8 in Valkey. Each `SETRANGE k 0 x` on a 512 MB string allocates and copies more than 1 GB transiently while holding the shard lock, stalling every other key in that shard.
suggested_fix: Store values in a growable buffer, or keep the value separate from the key so it can be extended in place.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_append (958-961) copies the current value with to_vec(), extends it, and replace_value (store.rs:224-235) copies the key and value again into a new Box, so every APPEND is O(len). cmd_setrange (1122-1141) copies the value twice even when only one byte changes, all under the shard lock. Valkey uses sdscatlen for APPEND (t_string.c:1130) and sdsgrowzero plus memcpy for SETRANGE (t_string.c:521-522). The reporter's Valkey estimate is too low: SDS_MAX_PREALLOC is 1MB, so above 1MB Valkey reallocates about every 1MB of growth, roughly 5e9 bytes for the 100MB build. That is still about 2000x less than rvk's roughly 1e13. This is a performance defect, not a wrong reply.

title: EXEC self-deadlocks on shard mutexes when a queued INFO or UNWATCH runs inside the transaction, which can hang the whole server
description: exec_transaction (cmd.rs:1556-1580) locks every shard used by the queued commands and by the client's WATCHed keys, then runs the queued handlers while it still holds those guards. Two handlers that can be queued then try to take the same std::sync::Mutex again on the same thread. cmd_info (cmd.rs:1957-1961) locks shards 0..63 one by one. cmd_unwatch -> unwatch_all (cmd.rs:1639-1641, 108-112) locks the shard of every watched key, and every one of those shards is held by EXEC. INFO and UNWATCH are flags 0 / Keys::None, so run_command queues them inside MULTI (cmd.rs:415-418). Valkey allows both inside MULTI (info.json and unwatch.json carry no NO_MULTI flag), and in Valkey UNWATCH under EXEC does nothing because execCommand has already unwatched (multi.c:361). std's futex Mutex is not reentrant, so the worker blocks forever and keeps its shard guards.
failure_scenario: An authenticated client (any client when requirepass is unset, as in the benchmark config) sends MULTI, SET k v, INFO, EXEC. Or it sends WATCH k, MULTI, UNWATCH, EXEC. EXEC holds shard_of(k), and INFO/UNWATCH then blocks on that same shard. The worker thread hangs for good, along with every connection it owns. Any other thread that later touches that shard also blocks: a command on a key there, INFO / KEYS / DBSIZE / FLUSHALL / RANDOMKEY (they lock all shards), random eviction in evict_one, and active expiry in cron for the owning worker. The server gradually stops responding entirely and has to be killed.
suggested_fix: Never take a shard lock from a handler that can run under EXEC. In exec_transaction, unwatch before running the queue, as Valkey does (multi.c:361), and make UNWATCH a no-op under EXEC. Have INFO read the lock-free counters, or reuse the guards in cx.locks when they are present. Add a debug assertion or helper so a handler cannot call store.lock() while Cx owns guards.
verifier_reasoning: Traced end to end. run_command (cmd.rs:408-418) queues INFO and UNWATCH inside MULTI: neither is NOMULTI, and neither is in the exec/discard/quit/reset exclusion list. exec_transaction (cmd.rs:1556-1580) collects the shards of the watched keys and of the keyed queued commands, then locks them with sh.store.lock(s) (std::sync::Mutex, store.rs:112-114). It moves those guards into cx.locks and calls (spec.run)(&mut cx) while still holding them (cmd.rs:1590-1611). cmd_info then calls sh.store.lock(i) for i in 0..NSHARDS (cmd.rs:1957-1958). cmd_unwatch calls unwatch_all, which runs store.lock(shard_of(key)) for every watched key (cmd.rs:108-112, 1639-1641). Every one of those shards is already held by the same thread. std Mutex is not reentrant: re-locking never returns, and the Linux futex implementation blocks forever. Both sequences hit it: MULTI, SET k v, INFO, EXEC, and WATCH k, MULTI, UNWATCH (or INFO), EXEC. The worker never comes back and keeps its guards, so any thread that later locks that shard also hangs: keyed commands, Keys::All commands, INFO, evict_one, and cron on the owning worker. Valkey allows INFO and UNWATCH in MULTI. Ordinary client code can trigger this by accident, not only an attacker.

title: DEBUG is enabled for every client, and DEBUG SLEEP inf (or 1e20) panics, which aborts the process
description: cmd_debug parses the SLEEP argument with Rust's f64 parser and passes secs.max(0.0) to Duration::from_secs_f64. Rust's parser accepts "inf" and "infinity", and from_secs_f64 panics on a non-finite value or one above u64::MAX seconds. The release profile sets panic = "abort", so the whole process dies. Even without the panic, DEBUG is open to every authenticated client, whereas Valkey defaults enable-debug-command to "no" (config.c:3548; server.c:4705 refuses it). DEBUG SLEEP with a large finite value blocks one worker thread indefinitely. SO_REUSEPORT keeps sending new connections to that worker's listener, and its cron (active expiry for its shards) stops running. Queued inside MULTI with keyed commands, the sleep runs while EXEC holds those shard locks, so every thread stalls. DEBUG SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE 0 can also be issued by any client.
failure_scenario: An authenticated client (anyone when no requirepass is set) sends DEBUG SLEEP inf or DEBUG SLEEP 1e20. from_secs_f64 panics, panic=abort kills the server, and all data is lost (there is no persistence). DEBUG SLEEP 1e18 hangs a worker and all of its present and future connections. MULTI, KEYS x, DEBUG SLEEP 1e18, EXEC holds all 64 shard locks for that time and freezes the whole server.
suggested_fix: Gate DEBUG behind an enable-debug-command option that defaults to no, as Valkey does. Parse SLEEP with Duration::try_from_secs_f64, or clamp to a finite maximum and reject non-finite input.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_debug (cmd.rs:2030-2032) parses with str::parse::<f64>, which accepts "inf" and "infinity". inf.max(0.0) is inf, and Duration::from_secs_f64 panics on a non-finite value or one above u64::MAX seconds, which covers 1e20. poc/Cargo.toml sets panic = "abort" in [profile.release], so the process aborts and the in-memory data is lost. DEBUG has no protection (lookup at cmd.rs:220, flags 0), while Valkey defaults enable-debug-command to no (config.c:3548, server.c:4705). Valkey's own DEBUG SLEEP with inf does not crash: it casts to long long and nanosleep fails. Severity is lowered for three reasons. An authenticated client can already kill both servers with SHUTDOWN (rvk cmd_shutdown is open to every authed client). The large-finite-sleep hang and the whole-server freeze inside MULTI are what Valkey also does once DEBUG is enabled. SET-ACTIVE-EXPIRE is the same. The real defects are the panic on parsed input and DEBUG being on by default.

title: Unauthenticated clients get neither of Valkey's buffer caps (1 MB query buffer, 1 KB output), so each one can hold 64 MB of output plus up to 2 GiB of input
description: Valkey bounds clients that have not authenticated in two places: the query buffer is capped at 1 MB (networking.c:4799-4802), and the output buffer of a never-authenticated client is capped at REPLY_BUFFER_SIZE_UNAUTHENTICATED_CLIENT = 1024 bytes, with disconnect (networking.c:6719-6721). rvk-server copies only the per-request limits (resp.rs:124, 151). on_readable applies the general client_query_buffer_limit (1 GiB default) whether or not the client is authenticated. process() appends a NOAUTH or unknown-command error for every pipelined request and has no output cap. Once wbuf exceeds OUTPUT_PAUSE (64 MB), process stops consuming input (server.rs:380-383), yet on_readable keeps reading and doubling rbuf. rbuf only stops when rlen passes 1 GiB, and by then it has been resized and zero-filled to 2 GiB (server.rs:319-323).
failure_scenario: With requirepass set, an unauthenticated client pipelines tiny requests (for example a 2-byte inline unknown command, which yields an error reply of about 55 bytes, about 27x amplification) and never reads its socket. Its wbuf grows to 64 MB, then its rbuf grows to 1-2 GiB before the connection is closed. A few such connections (maxclients defaults to 10000) exhaust host memory and get the server OOM-killed, without the attacker ever knowing the password.
suggested_fix: Mirror Valkey for unauthenticated clients. Close the connection once rlen exceeds 1 MB while !state.authed(), and once pending output exceeds 1 KB while the client has never authenticated.
verifier_reasoning: Valkey caps unauthenticated clients at a 1 MB query buffer (networking.c:4799-4802) and at 1024 bytes of output before disconnecting them (networking.c:6719-6721, server.h:235). rvk has neither cap. on_readable compares only against cfg.client_query_buffer_limit (server.rs:330). An unauthenticated client gets a NOAUTH or unknown-command error per pipelined request (cmd.rs:384-406), the connection is not closed, and wbuf has no cap. Once wbuf exceeds OUTPUT_PAUSE (64 MB), process breaks before parsing (server.rs:380-383). on_readable still drains the socket into rbuf, doubling it through resize (server.rs:319-323), and the shrink at server.rs:408 does not apply while rlen is large. Without the pause, an unauthenticated client's pending input is bounded (64 KB inline, 10 args of 16 KB). With the pause, it can grow up to the 1 GiB limit, and the zero-filled resize reaches 2 GiB before the close. About 2.4 MB of tiny requests builds the 64 MB of output, and the client can then park about 1 GiB of rbuf per connection. Pre-auth memory exhaustion that Valkey explicitly prevents.

title: maxmemory (DENYOOM) is never enforced on commands queued in MULTI or run by EXEC, and the queue is not counted toward the query-buffer limit
description: In run_command the MULTI branch queues the command and returns (cmd.rs:415-418) before the DENYOOM / make_room check (cmd.rs:421). EXEC itself is not DENYOOM, and exec_transaction calls the handlers directly without make_room. So no write executed through EXEC ever triggers eviction or an OOM rejection. Valkey checks OOM for each DENYOOM command, including at queue time, and rejects EXEC when the queued commands include DENYOOM ones (server.c:4731, 4881, using combined_flags with the mstate flags). Valkey also counts the queued argv bytes against client-query-buffer-limit (networking.c:4800). rvk's Multi.queued (Vec<Vec<Vec<u8>>>) is limited by nothing.
failure_scenario: With --maxmemory 256mb --maxmemory-policy noeviction, a client wraps its writes as MULTI, SET k1 <big>, SET k2 <big>, ..., EXEC. Every SET succeeds and memory grows without limit past maxmemory until the process is OOM-killed. Under allkeys-lru, the same transactions never evict, so the configured memory limit is silently ignored. A client can also queue millions of commands without ever sending EXEC; the queued copies are counted against neither maxmemory nor client-query-buffer-limit. This also gives an unfair benchmark advantage, because transactional writes skip the eviction work that Valkey performs.
suggested_fix: Run the DENYOOM / make_room check before queueing, as Valkey does. Record the union of flags in Multi, and in exec_transaction run make_room / reject with OOM when any queued command is DENYOOM. Track the queued argv byte total and include it in the client_query_buffer_limit check.
verifier_reasoning: In run_command, the MULTI branch pushes the command into m.queued and returns at cmd.rs:415-418, before the DENYOOM/make_room check at cmd.rs:421. EXEC's spec is NOMULTI only, with no DENYOOM. exec_transaction calls handlers directly and never calls make_room, and run_command is never invoked with in_exec=true, so no write inside EXEC evicts or is rejected for OOM. Valkey runs performEvictions and the OOM rejection (server.c:4868-4890) before queueMultiCommand (server.c:5025). At EXEC it uses combined_flags, which include the mstate DENYOOM flags (server.c:4724-4731). Multi.queued (cmd.rs:69-72) is not limited by anything. Valkey counts mstate->argv_len_sums against client-query-buffer-limit (networking.c:4800). Under noeviction, MULTI/SET big.../EXEC grows past maxmemory without limit. Client libraries that wrap pipelines in MULTI/EXEC by default (for example redis-py transaction=True) reach this with ordinary traffic.

title: An incomplete multibulk request is re-parsed from its first argument on every read event, so large-argc requests cost quadratic CPU
description: resp::parse keeps no state between calls. Each time process() is called (on every readable event, server.rs:384), parsing restarts at the start of the pending command, clears ranges (resp.rs:101), and walks every argument received so far (resp.rs:131-164) before returning Incomplete. Valkey keeps multibulklen/bulklen/argc in the client and resumes where it stopped, so its parsing is linear. An authenticated client may send any count up to i32::MAX (any client may when requirepass is unset), with the query buffer limited to 1 GiB.
failure_scenario: A client announces a multibulk of a few million small arguments (for example an MGET or DEL of 1-byte keys, about 7 bytes per argument) and sends it in many small TCP segments. With k arguments already buffered, each read event costs O(k). For N arguments delivered in N/c events the total is about N^2/(2c) argument parses. With N = 10M and 1460-byte segments that is on the order of 10^11 parse steps, so one worker thread runs at 100% CPU for minutes, and every other connection on that worker stalls meanwhile. Valkey handles the same input in linear time.
suggested_fix: Keep parse progress in the connection (number of args parsed, offset of the next header, pending bulk length) and resume from it instead of restarting at pos. Alternatively, when the previous parse returned Incomplete, skip re-parsing until the expected bulk end has arrived.
verifier_reasoning: resp::parse is stateless. Each call clears ranges (resp.rs:101) and loops over every argument from the start of the pending command (resp.rs:131-164) before returning Incomplete at the first missing one. process() calls it once per readable event (server.rs:384), and again from on_writable/process_and_flush, so parse work grows with the number of arguments already buffered. Nothing caches progress, and count may be up to i32::MAX for authed clients (resp.rs:11, 120-126). Each argument costs a short memchr plus parse_i64. With millions of small arguments delivered across many read events, the total work is O(N^2/c) and the thread is pinned. Valkey keeps multibulklen/bulklen in the client and parses linearly. The 'every other connection stalls' wording overstates it slightly: they are delayed per event (tens of ms at k in the millions), not blocked outright. The quadratic CPU cost is real, and large legitimate MSET/DEL requests over slow links also pay it.

title: WATCH checks for duplicate keys by scanning a Vec, so WATCH costs O(n^2) while holding every shard lock it touches
description: cmd_watch tests each key against conn.watched with a linear iter().any() (cmd.rs:1628), so WATCH with n keys does O(n^2) byte-slice comparisons. WATCH is KALL1, so lock_for has already taken the mutex of every shard the keys hash to. With more than a few hundred distinct keys that is all 64 shards. Every scan of the list also covers keys added by earlier WATCH calls. Valkey uses a per-client hashtable for this check (multi.c:505), which is O(1) per key.
failure_scenario: An authenticated client sends one WATCH with about 300k distinct keys (a few MB request). That is about 4.5x10^10 key comparisons, run while the client holds all 64 shard mutexes. For that whole period every other worker thread blocks on its first keyed command, INFO, or eviction, so the entire server freezes for tens of seconds per request. Repeating the request keeps the freeze going.
suggested_fix: Keep the connection's watched keys in a HashSet (or check the shard's watched map for this flag) so the duplicate test is O(1). Consider capping the number of watched keys per connection.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_watch checks cx.conn.watched.iter().any(|k| k == key) for each argument (cmd.rs:1628), a linear scan over a Vec that also holds keys from earlier WATCH calls, so n keys cost O(n^2) comparisons. WATCH's spec is KALL1 (cmd.rs:206), so lock_for locks every distinct shard of the keys before the handler runs (cmd.rs:469-491). With hundreds of distinct keys that is all 64 shards, and they stay held for the whole quadratic loop, so every other worker blocks on its next keyed, Keys::All or eviction lock. Valkey checks the per-client hashtable watched_keys_by_db in O(1) (multi.c:505). With about 300k keys, about 4.5e10 comparisons is minutes of global freeze, if anything worse than the reporter estimated. Requires an authenticated client.

title: APPEND, SETRANGE and GETRANGE copy the entire value (two or three times) on each call while holding the shard lock
description: cmd_append copies the whole current value with to_vec() and extends it (cmd.rs:958-959). replace_value then builds another full key+value Vec before the old value is freed (store.rs:224-232). cmd_setrange copies the whole value too (cmd.rs:1122-1125), including the empty-value case where it only needs the length (cmd.rs:1126-1127), and then goes through replace_value again. cmd_getrange copies the whole value to return a slice of it (cmd.rs:1090). Valkey does APPEND/SETRANGE in place with amortized sdsMakeRoomFor, and GETRANGE in O(range). All of these copies run under the shard mutex, and the temporary 2-3x of the value size is not counted toward maxmemory.
failure_scenario: With a 512 MB value at key k, each GETRANGE k 0 0 allocates and memcpys 512 MB to return one byte. A pipeline of them from several clients spikes RSS by multiples of 512 MB and blocks every command on that shard. Building a large value through repeated 1 KB APPENDs costs O(len) per append (about 2.7x10^14 bytes copied to reach 512 MB), against linear cost in Valkey. A single SETRANGE k 536870000 x on a large key briefly needs about 3x the value size, which can push the process past maxmemory and into the OOM killer.
suggested_fix: Slice the value in place for GETRANGE and reply directly from the slab, as reply_value does. For APPEND and SETRANGE, mutate the slot's buffer in place (store values in a growable Vec with amortized capacity, or realloc the Box) instead of copying the whole value twice.
verifier_reasoning: cmd_append copies the whole value with to_vec() and extends it (cmd.rs:958-959). replace_value then allocates and copies key plus value again (store.rs:224-232) while the old data is still alive, so each append costs O(len) and building a value by appends is quadratic. Valkey appends in place with amortized sdsMakeRoomFor. cmd_getrange copies the whole value to return a sub-slice (cmd.rs:1090), O(value) instead of O(range). cmd_setrange copies the whole value even when val is empty and only the length is needed (cmd.rs:1122-1127), then goes through replace_value or set, which allocates another copy. All of this runs under the shard mutex. One overstatement: the GETRANGE temporaries for one key are serialized by its shard lock, so the RSS spikes multiply only across keys on different shards. The quadratic APPEND and the O(N) GETRANGE amplification are real.

title: The read buffer grows by doubling past client_query_buffer_limit and is zero-filled to 2x the limit before the limit check
description: on_readable doubles rbuf (resize writes zeros, which commits the pages) whenever it is full, and checks rlen > client_query_buffer_limit only after the next read. Buffer sizes are 16 KiB x 2^k, so with the default 1 GiB limit the buffer fills to exactly 1 GiB (not over the limit, because the check is strictly greater), is resized to 2 GiB, and only after that read is the connection closed. A single large argument also costs up to 2x its size, because a 512 MB bulk lands in a 1 GiB buffer. Valkey grows the query buffer in bounded steps and allocates big arguments at their exact size.
failure_scenario: A client streams a request that never completes, for example a 512 MB bulk followed by more data, or simply over 1 GiB of pipelined input while its output is paused. The worker allocates and zero-fills a 2 GiB buffer for that one connection, twice the configured limit. Several such connections in parallel exceed host memory well before the configured limits suggest.
suggested_fix: Cap new_len at client_query_buffer_limit + READ_CHUNK (or close when rlen + avail would exceed the limit) before resizing. For known large bulk lengths, reserve exactly start+len+2 instead of doubling, and use reserve instead of a zero-filling resize.
verifier_reasoning: on_readable resizes rbuf to twice its size, zero-filled, whenever rlen == rbuf.len() (server.rs:319-323), and checks rlen > limit only after the next read (server.rs:330). Sizes are 16 KiB x 2^k, so with the default 1 GiB limit the buffer is exactly 1 GiB. rlen can never exceed that limit without first resizing to 2 GiB. Vec::resize writes zeros, which commits the new half, and realloc may briefly hold the old buffer as well. A 512 MB bulk also needs the 1 GiB buffer, then make_data copies it into the store. Valkey grows its query buffer to about limit plus one read and stores big arguments without a copy. Severity is low because this is a 2x overshoot of a per-connection limit that authenticated Valkey clients can already approach. The unauthenticated amplification belongs to finding 2.

title: requirepass is compared with a non-constant-time slice equality
description: check_password compares with p.as_slice() == pass, which returns early on a length mismatch and on the first differing byte. AUTH and HELLO ... AUTH both use it, before the client is authenticated. Valkey hashes the candidate with SHA-256 and compares with time_independent_strcmp (acl.c:226, 1983), so its comparison time does not depend on the password.
failure_scenario: A network attacker who can time many AUTH attempts (there is no rate limit) gets a timing signal that depends on the password's length and on how long a prefix matches. That makes a remote length/prefix side channel possible against requirepass, which Valkey's design closes.
suggested_fix: Compare in constant time: hash both sides with SHA-256 and fold the XOR of the digests, or use a constant-time comparison over equal-length buffers. Keep the user-name check separate from the timing-sensitive path.
verifier_reasoning: check_password does compare with p.as_slice() == pass (cmd.rs:1691), and Valkey compares SHA-256 digests with time_independent_strcmp (acl.c:226, 1980-1983). That is a real hardening gap. However, Rust slice equality is a length check followed by memcmp/bcmp, and glibc's vectorized memcmp compares passwords of 32 bytes or less in one overlapping vector compare. It works in 32 to 128-byte blocks beyond that, not byte by byte, so the per-prefix leak described does not exist for normal passwords. What remains is a nanosecond-scale difference on the length check, well below remote network timing resolution. The failure the report describes, an attacker recovering length or prefix information, is not shown to happen.

title: Argument offsets and key lengths are stored as u32, so large configured limits truncate them into a panic or silent data corruption
description: ArgRange stores start/end as u32 (start as u32, end as u32 at resp.rs:162), and Slot.klen is key.len() as u32 (store.rs:211). Both --client-query-buffer-limit and --proto-max-bulk-len accept arbitrary sizes such as 8gb, and Valkey supports such settings. Once the read buffer or a single argument goes beyond 4 GiB, offsets wrap: Args::get can build a range with end < start, which panics and with panic=abort kills the server, or it can return the wrong bytes. A key longer than 4 GiB stores the wrong key/value split.
failure_scenario: The operator raises the limits (for example --client-query-buffer-limit 8gb --proto-max-bulk-len 6gb). A client then sends SET k with a 4.5 GB value. ArgRange.end wraps below start, Args::get slices &buf[start..end] with start > end, and the process aborts. With other offsets, a different byte range is stored silently.
suggested_fix: Use usize (or u64) for ArgRange offsets and Slot.klen, or reject at startup any proto-max-bulk-len / client-query-buffer-limit that does not fit in u32.
verifier_reasoning: ArgRange stores start as u32 and end as u32 (resp.rs:24-28, 162), and Slot.klen = key.len() as u32 (store.rs:211). main.rs parse_memory accepts any size for --proto-max-bulk-len and --client-query-buffer-limit with no cap, and Valkey allows both up to LONG_MAX (config.c:3648, 3669). With a 6 GB bulk limit and an 8 GB query buffer limit, SET k with a 4.5e9-byte value parses with start of about 30 and end = start + 4.5e9, which truncates to about 205 MB. Args::get then returns &buf[30..205032734], so a truncated value is stored silently. Specific lengths near 2^32, or offsets past 4 GiB in a pipelined buffer, make end < start, which panics and aborts under panic=abort. Low severity because it needs non-default operator settings above 4 GiB.

title: Valkey runs per-command observability bookkeeping in call() and beforeSleep(); rvk only bumps one counter
failure_scenario: read90-p16 or mixed50-p16 at 50 connections. Valkey spends roughly 3-8% of its per-op CPU on hdr_record_value, commandstats, duration samples and beforeSleep timing. rvk does none of this. The reported throughput and CPU/op gap is inflated by that amount on top of any architectural difference.
suggested_fix: Add a Valkey sensitivity run with `--latency-tracking no` (removes the histogram) and report rvk's lead with and without it. State that the rest of call()'s bookkeeping is a structural Valkey cost that rvk does not have because commandstats, latencystats and commandlog are out of scope. Alternatively, give rvk per-command calls/usec counters so INFO commandstats can be compared.
verifier_reasoning: The code matches the claim. On every call, Valkey's call() runs ustime() and two getMonotonicUs() (server.c:4201-4214, 4263-4269), durationAddSample (4313-4318), commandlogPushCurrentCommand (4325), the monitor feed check (4330-4334), calls/microseconds (4339-4340), updateCommandLatencyHistogram->hdr_record_value (4341-4342, 3978-3985) and the zmalloc_used_memory peak sample (4413-4414). latency-tracking defaults to 1 (config.c:3488), and harness.py:108-112 never passes --latency-tracking no. rvk's run_command does only Stats::add (cmd.rs:382) and now_ms (cmd.rs:431). The measured profile backs this up: results/profile2/valkey-1t-p16.top-symbols.txt shows getMonotonicUs_x86 5.02%, call 3.41% and commandlogPushEntryIfNeeded 0.77%; at p1, getMonotonicUs is 0.97% and call 0.55%. So the reporter's statement that the clock reads are cheap is wrong: they are the largest single item. Not every getMonotonicUs call is observability, though, since aeProcessEvents timers use it too. The bias toward rvk is real, about 1-2% at p1 and about 5% or more at p16. I downgrade it to low because it changes no result's direction. rvk-1t is already 0.73-0.96x valkey-1t (summary_part2.md), and rvk-2t's roughly 12% CPU/op lead over valkey-2shard at p1 shrinks but survives.

title: Valkey enables TCP keepalive on every accepted socket (4 setsockopt calls); rvk sets neither keepalive nor an idle timeout
description:
Valkey's accept handler calls anetKeepAlive for every new connection (socket.c:349), because tcp-keepalive defaults to 300 (config.c:3574). That is four setsockopt calls (anet.c:154-222: SO_KEEPALIVE, TCP_KEEPIDLE, TCP_KEEPINTVL, TCP_KEEPCNT), on top of accept4 and TCP_NODELAY. SO_KEEPALIVE and TCP_KEEPIDLE each take the socket lock and re-arm the keepalive timer.

rvk's accept_all only calls set_nodelay (server.rs:271-272). rvk has no keepalive and no idle timeout anywhere: CONFIG GET reports timeout 0 (cmd.rs:1857), and the connection struct does not track last activity.

Estimated cost: about 0.8-1.5 us of extra syscall work per connection, roughly 3-6% of the 20-40 us of server CPU per connection in a churn workload. This only matters for get100-churn (harness.py:286), which opens a new TCP connection for every request. Keepalive is not optional in a real deployment: it is how Valkey detects dead peers.
failure_scenario:
1) Benchmark: in get100-churn, each request costs Valkey four more setsockopt syscalls than rvk, so rvk's connection-churn advantage is overstated by a few percent.
2) Deployment: a client host crashes or a NAT/LB silently drops the flow without sending FIN or RST. rvk keeps the Conn with its 16 KB rbuf and 16 KB wbuf, plus its `connected` count, forever. Enough of these exhaust maxclients (10000) and every new client gets '-ERR max number of clients reached'. Valkey's default keepalive reaps such peers after about 300 s plus the probe time.
suggested_fix: In accept_all, set SO_KEEPALIVE, TCP_KEEPIDLE=300, TCP_KEEPINTVL and TCP_KEEPCNT through socket2::SockRef::set_tcp_keepalive, matching Valkey's defaults. As a sensitivity control, run get100-churn with Valkey `--tcp-keepalive 0` and report both numbers.
verifier_reasoning: On every accept, Valkey calls anetKeepAlive (socket.c:349) because tcp-keepalive defaults to 300 (config.c:3574). That makes 4 setsockopt calls on Linux (anet.c:154-222). rvk's accept_all only calls set_nodelay (server.rs:271-272). rvk has no keepalive or idle-timeout code anywhere: CONFIG GET timeout is hard-coded to 0 (cmd.rs:1857), Conn has no activity timestamp (server.rs:131-139), and main.rs has no keepalive option. Benchmark effect: get100-churn is client-bound at equal throughput, and server CPU/op is 37.55 us for valkey-1t vs 32.02 us for rvk-1t (summary_part2.md:337-339). Four extra syscalls, about 1 us, plausibly explain a few percent of that gap. Deployment effect: a peer that vanishes without FIN/RST, on an idle connection with no pending output, never produces an epoll event under rvk. The Conn (16 KB zeroed rbuf plus 16 KB wbuf capacity) and its `connected` slot are held forever, and enough of them eventually trip the maxclients check (server.rs:274). Valkey reaps such peers through keepalive. The path is traced end to end.

title: Valkey accounts memory on every allocation and free; rvk uses a 100 ms jemalloc snapshot plus an estimate, which is cheaper but blind to non-dataset growth between snapshots
description:
Every Valkey zmalloc and zfree calls je_malloc_usable_size and updates a per-thread counter (zmalloc.c:126-133, 172-189). A GET does about 4 such events (argv objects for the command name and key, then their frees). A SET does about 8-10 (argv objects, re-allocating the object to embed the key, and freeing the old value on overwrite). That is about 20-60 ns per op, and Valkey pays it even with maxmemory 0, where it only feeds INFO used_memory.

rvk does no per-allocation accounting:
- Rust uses sized deallocation, so frees skip the usable-size lookup.
- maxmemory uses jemalloc stats.allocated, refreshed by each thread's cron (cmd.rs:616-620), plus the store's own estimate between refreshes (cmd.rs:498-506). That estimate charges key+value+56 bytes per entry (store.rs:23-26, 48-50).

Allocations outside the store estimate stay invisible until the next cron (up to 1/hz = 100 ms per thread):
- per-connection wbuf and rbuf growth;
- stale expiry-heap entries, up to 2×volatile+4096 per shard (store.rs:335);
- slab Vec and hashbrown capacity doubling.

The cost advantage is small: about 0.3-1% non-pipelined and a few percent at pipeline 16. In return rvk gets less precise accounting, which FEATURE_MATRIX §5 already shows as 0.2-0.3% overshoot against Valkey's 0.02%, but only for a uniform-SET test. In the evict-* workloads the two servers hold different numbers of resident keys (FEATURE_MATRIX §5 says rvk holds fewer), so GET hit ratio and evictions per SET differ. Results that do not report hit ratio are not like-for-like.
failure_scenario: maxmemory 256mb allkeys-lru, 1000 clients pipelining 16 GETs of 16 KB values while writers run. About 256 KB of wbuf per connection, roughly 250 MB in total, can appear within one 100 ms cron window. Until the next jemalloc refresh, make_room only sees the dataset-estimate delta, so SETs run without evicting and RSS overshoots maxmemory by about that amount. Valkey counts each reply-buffer allocation immediately and evicts on the next command.
suggested_fix: Track connection-buffer capacity changes (rbuf/wbuf grow and shrink) and expiry-heap capacity in a per-thread atomic that used_memory() adds, so the estimate between crons includes them. Report hit ratio and resident key count next to throughput for evict-uniform and evict-skew.
verifier_reasoning: The mechanism is real but it is not a defect or an unfair advantage. FEATURE_MATRIX.md §5 documents it exactly: jemalloc stats.allocated refreshed every 100 ms plus the store estimate in between, marked partial, with the measured overshoot. The report says results that omit hit ratio are not like-for-like, but the Part II results do report hit rate and evictions for the evict workloads (results/summary_part2.md:317: valkey-1t 0.323, rvk 0.279). The overshoot scenario is bounded by one cron tick (cmd.rs:616-620, run every 1/hz per thread). Once the snapshot includes the wbuf/rbuf allocations, make_room evicts just as Valkey does: Valkey also counts normal-client output buffers in used_memory, so it would evict the same dataset. The only difference is a lag of at most 100 ms. The per-allocation accounting cost in Valkey is an implementation-efficiency difference for an in-scope feature, not skipped work. je_malloc_usable_size is also used to give sds its usable capacity, so not all of that profile time is accounting.

title: Valkey hashes keys and command names with keyed SipHash on every lookup; rvk uses foldhash::fast and a compiled command match
description:
Valkey's keys and expires tables hash with SipHash under a random or configured seed (server.c:439-444, 704-728). A GET does 1 SipHash. A SET does 2-4: lookupKeyWrite, the FindRef in dbSetValue, and the FindRef and expires-table Add in setExpire (db.c:1964-1998). Command lookup adds a case-insensitive SipHash (server.c:732-733).

rvk uses foldhash::fast::RandomState (store.rs:17, 96-102), twice per keyed command (cmd.rs:461 and cmd.rs:279), and dispatches commands through a compiled match (cmd.rs:154-226).

Estimated difference: about 15-50 ns per op, roughly 0.2-1.5% non-pipelined. Part of it is Valkey re-hashing the same key, a legitimate efficiency win for rvk. The rest is hash strength. Keyed SipHash is Valkey's defence against hash flooding with untrusted keys; foldhash is documented as non-cryptographic and only 'minimally DoS-resistant'. rvk also takes the shard from bits of the same hash (store.rs:107-109). If an attacker finds colliding keys, they degrade hashbrown probing and also pile onto a single shard mutex.
failure_scenario: A client that can choose key names, such as a cache keyed on user input, finds a set of keys that collide under foldhash. Lookups in one shard degrade, and every worker thread queues on that shard's Mutex. Valkey's keyed SipHash makes such sets impractical to construct. In benchmarks the cheaper hash is credited to rvk even though it provides weaker protection.
suggested_fix: Run one sensitivity benchmark with rvk using a keyed SipHash (std RandomState, SipHash-1-3) to quantify how much of the gap comes from the hash, and record the security trade in THREAT_MODEL.md. Hash each key once per command and pass h from lock_for into Cx::find.
verifier_reasoning: The facts are correct. rvk uses foldhash::fast::RandomState (store.rs:17, 96-102) and hashes the key twice (cmd.rs:461, 279). Valkey uses seeded SipHash plus siphash_nocase for the command lookup, about 2% in the p16 profile. A cheaper hash and a compiled match dispatch are legitimate implementation efficiencies, though, not skipped functionality. The DoS scenario is not traced. Both servers use a per-process random seed, and the report gives no way for an attacker who cannot see hash outputs to build colliding key sets for foldhash, or keys that land in one shard via bits 40-45 (store.rs:107-109). 'If an attacker finds colliding keys' is the speculative premise the rules exclude.

title: Valkey rewrites every SET ... EX into SET ... PXAT for propagation even with no replicas or AOF; rvk's TTL path is a heap push
description:
For `SET k v EX s`, the form the loadgen sends (bench/rust/loadgen/src/main.rs:227, 623-625), setGenericCommand always does the following (t_string.c:176-191):
- creates a timestamp object (createStringObjectFromLongLong);
- calls rewriteClientCommandArgument twice, which allocates a new argv array, keeps original_argv, and churns 5 refcounts (networking.c:6479-6516).
All of this is freed in resetClient, even though shouldPropagate later finds no AOF and no replicas (server.c:3787-3799). setExpire also does a second main-table FindRef and, for new keys, an expires-table insert (db.c:1964-1998).

rvk's SET EX overwrites the slot and pushes (expire, hash) onto a per-shard min-heap (store.rs:191-221). With a constant TTL the new deadline is the largest, so the push is usually O(1).

Estimated cost: about 50-100 ns per SET EX, or about 25-50 ns per op averaged over ttl-mixed50 (50% SET EX). That is under 1% non-pipelined. The work is replication/AOF bookkeeping, which is out of rvk's scope, so it is operational overhead.

The heap design itself is legitimate (declared partial in FEATURE_MATRIX §4). However, its cost lands in tail latency, not throughput: each overwrite of a volatile key leaves a stale entry. When len > 2×volatile+4096, maybe_compact_heap rebuilds the shard's heap in O(n), re-hashing every volatile key while holding the shard mutex (store.rs:334-344).
failure_scenario: ttl-mixed50 (SET EX 5 on a 1M keyspace, about 15.6K keys per shard). Every SET EX costs Valkey 2-3 allocations plus frees and refcount churn for a propagation vector nobody consumes, and this is counted against Valkey. Meanwhile each rvk shard periodically blocks every thread touching it for about 100-200 us during the heap rebuild. A throughput-only comparison shows rvk's advantage but hides the rebuild stall.
suggested_fix: Report ttl-mixed50 with p99/p99.9 latency, not only throughput, and note that Valkey's PXAT rewrite is propagation overhead outside rvk's scope. Optionally make rvk's heap compaction incremental (rebuild in budgeted chunks, or compact during cron) instead of inline in SET.
verifier_reasoning: The Valkey side is accurate: t_string.c:176-191 rewrites SET ... EX to PXAT unconditionally, and shouldPropagate later drops it (server.c:3787-3799). But it is Valkey-inherent replication work that no configuration removes, and by the reporter's own estimate it is under 1%. The rvk half of the scenario does not happen. maybe_compact_heap fires only when heap len > 2*volatile+4096 (store.rs:335). In ttl-mixed50, rvk-2t runs at 272K ops/s (summary_part2.md:283), so about 136K SET EX/s, about 2.1K per shard per second. Cron pops due entries every 100 ms (cmd.rs:604-613), so the heap holds about 5 s of pushes, about 10.7K. Volatile is about 15.6K*(1-e^-0.68), about 7.7K, so the threshold is about 19.5K. The rebuild needs roughly 3x the measured throughput, so the claimed 100-200 us per-shard stall does not occur in that workload.

title: rvk has no output-buffer cap for unauthenticated clients, so such clients can drive used_memory over maxmemory and evict the whole dataset
description:
Valkey disconnects a client that has never authenticated once its pending output exceeds 1024 bytes (networking.c:6719-6722, server.h:235). It also caps such a client's query buffer at 1 MB (networking.c:4800-4803).

rvk answers each unauthenticated command with NOAUTH and keeps reading and executing (cmd.rs:400-407). Pending output only pauses processing at 64 MB per connection (server.rs:28-29, 379-383), and nothing ever disconnects. The read limit is client_query_buffer_limit, 1 GB by default, and it applies regardless of auth state (server.rs:330-332).

Wbuf memory enters used_memory through the jemalloc snapshot (cmd.rs:616-620). From that point, make_room keeps evicting (cmd.rs:516-542).

Valkey only checks the limit once a client's 16 KB static reply buffer overflows into the reply list (networking.c:6786-6795). The check therefore costs nothing on the benchmark path, so this item does not change the measured comparison. It is a case of rvk doing less than a deployment with requirepass needs. FEATURE_MATRIX §1 documents the missing client-output-buffer-limit, but not this unauthenticated cap.
failure_scenario:
requirepass set, maxmemory 256mb allkeys-lru, 1M keys loaded.
1. An attacker without the password opens 10 connections and pipelines `PING\r\n` continuously without reading.
2. Each 6-byte request produces a 35-byte NOAUTH error, so each wbuf grows to about 64 MB, about 640 MB in total.
3. After the next cron, used_memory exceeds 256 MB, and every authenticated SET evicts up to 64 keys until the dataset is empty.
4. With nothing left to evict, make_room returns false and SETs get OOM errors.
The result is cache wipe and write denial of service without credentials. Valkey closes each of these connections after about 16 KB of pending output.
suggested_fix: Close a connection that is not authenticated once its pending output exceeds about 1 KB beyond the first chunk (mirror REPLY_BUFFER_SIZE_UNAUTHENTICATED_CLIENT), and cap rlen at 1 MB while not authenticated.
verifier_reasoning: Valkey closes a never-authenticated client once output exceeds REPLY_BUFFER_SIZE_UNAUTHENTICATED_CLIENT (1024) beyond the static buffer (networking.c:6719-6722, server.h:235). It also caps such a client's query buffer at 1 MB (networking.c:4800-4803). rvk replies NOAUTH and keeps processing (cmd.rs:400-407). Output only pauses at 64 MB (server.rs:29, 379-383) and never disconnects. While paused, on_readable keeps reading into rbuf until client_query_buffer_limit, 1 GB by default (server.rs:318-332, main.rs:56), so the exposure is worse than reported. The global allocator is jemalloc (main.rs:20-21), so these buffers enter the cron snapshot (cmd.rs:616-620). From then on, make_room evicts on every DENYOOM command until it reaches EVICT_FAIL-equivalent and returns OOM (cmd.rs:516-541). The parser's unauthenticated limits (resp.rs:124, 151) do not stop pipelined inline PINGs. This is a pre-auth cache wipe and memory DoS when requirepass is set, so I rate it medium. It has no benchmark impact.

title: rvk skips the eviction and OOM check for MULTI/EXEC and for commands not flagged DENYOOM
description:
In run_command, a command inside MULTI is queued and the function returns (cmd.rs:408-420) before the make_room call at cmd.rs:421. EXEC is flagged NOMULTI but not DENYOOM, so make_room never runs for it either. exec_transaction then runs the queued SETs directly with no memory check (cmd.rs:1539-1620). The `in_exec` parameter is always false.

Valkey's processCommand calls performEvictions for every command when maxmemory is set, including commands being queued and EXEC (server.c:4868-4897). It rejects an EXEC whose accumulated flags include DENYOOM with EXECABORT/OOM.

rvk also never evicts while traffic is read-only, whereas Valkey evicts on any command once over the limit. This has no effect on the GET/SET benchmark matrix, which does not use transactions. It is still a case of rvk doing less than Valkey semantics and a memory bound require, and it allows unbounded memory use.
failure_scenario: CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy noeviction, then fill until a plain SET returns '-OOM command not allowed...'. Then send MULTI, followed by SET k1 <100B> ... SET k100000 <100B>, then EXEC. All 100000 SETs succeed and memory grows past maxmemory without bound. Valkey replies EXECABORT with OOM. Under allkeys-lru, a client that writes only through transactions never triggers eviction. After CONFIG SET maxmemory is lowered, read-only traffic leaves rvk over the limit indefinitely.
suggested_fix: Call make_room before queuing a DENYOOM command inside MULTI, and set m.errored on OOM. Also call it at EXEC when any queued command is DENYOOM, returning EXECABORT on failure. Consider running the cheap used <= max check for every keyed command, as Valkey does.
verifier_reasoning: Inside MULTI, run_command queues and returns at cmd.rs:415-418, before the make_room check at cmd.rs:421. EXEC is flagged NOMULTI only (cmd.rs:204), so make_room never runs for it. exec_transaction calls spec.run directly with no memory check (cmd.rs:1591-1611). run_command's only caller passes in_exec=false (cmd.rs:352). Valkey runs performEvictions for every command when maxmemory is set (server.c:4868-4869). It rejects with OOM when is_denyoom_command is set (server.c:4880-4886), which covers a queued SET (DENYOOM) and EXEC through combined mstate flags (server.c:4722-4731). The rejection flags the transaction, so EXEC aborts. Result: under noeviction, MULTI/SET.../EXEC succeeds in rvk past the limit, repeatably and without bound. Under allkeys-lru, writes made only through transactions never trigger eviction. Read-only traffic never evicts either, whereas Valkey also has the eviction timer started by CONFIG SET maxmemory. This breaks the in-scope maxmemory bound, so I rate it above low.

title: Costs rvk pays that Valkey does not, which partly offset the items above
failure_scenario: rvk-2t on get100. Every GET does a relaxed store to mem[shard]. The cache line holding that shard's counter (shared with 7 other shards) is alternately owned by the two cores, adding about 50-100 ns of coherence traffic on most GETs that a single-threaded Valkey never pays. rvk's measured CPU/op is higher than its design requires, which masks part of the Valkey-side bias.
suggested_fix: Publish mem only when it changed (skip for reads), pad each shard's AtomicUsize to its own cache line, reuse an argv Vec held in ThreadCtx and avoid cloning it in cmd_set, pass the hash from lock_for into Cx::find, and allocate rbuf without zeroing (or lazily).
verifier_reasoning: finish() calls publish_mem for every locked shard on every keyed command, GET included, even when mem is unchanged (cmd.rs:437-451, store.rs:118-120). Store.mem is an unpadded Box<[AtomicUsize]> of 64 entries, 8 per 64-byte line (store.rs:77, 95). With 2 threads hitting random shards, the 8 lines ping-pong between cores. The guard drop that follows (Rust's futex Mutex unlock is an xchg) drains the store buffer, which exposes the RFO latency. The rvk-2t-p16 profile shows 3.13% in drop_glue of Locks, consistent with this. used_memory sums all 64 counters on each DENYOOM command when maxmemory is set (cmd.rs:498-518, store.rs:123-125). The per-command argv Vec (cmd.rs:351), the clone in cmd_set (cmd.rs:815), the double hash (cmd.rs:461/279), the zeroed 16 KB rbuf (server.rs:291) and the absent prefetch (Valkey networking.c:4683) are all as described. This is a real, if small, inefficiency that biases results against rvk, not toward it.

title: Valkey per-command items checked and found negligible or matched by rvk (not a bias)
failure_scenario: No defect. This is listed so a reader does not credit rvk's throughput lead to skipping keyspace notifications, tracking, ACL, output-buffer-limit or LRU work. On the benchmark path those are flag checks in Valkey, or rvk does the same work.
suggested_fix: None required. Cite this list in BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md when explaining where the Valkey/rvk per-op difference comes from.

The parity and gated-check observations I spot-checked are consistent with the code: watched.is_empty() (store.rs:362-365), LRU touch (store.rs:183-187), hits/misses (cmd.rs:311-317), lazy expiry (store.rs:170-179) and the query-limit check (server.rs:330-332).
